course.title: AI Agents and Agent Architecture
course.description: Design agents you can trust: the loop, tools and protocols, memory, patterns for planning and composition, and the controls for permissions, injection, traces, evaluation and oversight.
course.audience: A developer who has called a language model from code. ai-engineering (tokens, prompts, retrieval, evaluation) is the recommended earlier course. Coding assistants are covered separately in ai-assisted-engineering.

paragraphs: Give a language model a goal, a set of tools and a loop, and it becomes an agent: at each step it reads everything that has happened so far, chooses a tool, and reads the result before it chooses again. An agent asked to deal with a damaged order might look the order up, read the refund policy, issue a refund and write to the customer, and nobody wrote that sequence in advance, because the model chose each step as it went. That freedom is what lets an agent handle a request that no programmer anticipated, and it is also the source of almost every difficulty in building one.

Much of the engineering follows from that one fact. A run whose length the model decides has a cost, a duration and a chance of failure that the code around the model has to bound, and since each step re-reads everything before it, the cost grows faster than the number of steps. An agent that reads email or web pages is also reading text that strangers wrote, which it cannot reliably tell apart from its user's instructions, so what it is permitted to do has to be enforced outside the model, where no sentence can argue with the rule.

The subject is often argued in terms of how capable a model seems, yet most of its questions can be settled with arithmetic on a design you can see. Multiplying the success rate of one step by itself tells you how often a ten-step run finishes, adding up the context a loop re-reads tells you what a run will cost, and multiplying a refund cap by a rate limit tells you the most money that can leave in a day without anyone approving it. Those numbers are what let you decide how much freedom an agent should have, and what evidence would justify giving it more.
outcomes: You'll be able to choose between a workflow, a copilot and an agent for a task.
You'll be able to trace an agent loop and compute its cost and reliability.
You'll be able to design tools and a server-side permission model.
You'll be able to recognise prompt injection and break the lethal trifecta.
You'll be able to instrument and evaluate an agent and stage its rollout.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on Python for Data Analysis, How Computers Solve Problems, Probability and Statistics, AI Engineering: LLMs, Prompting, Retrieval and Evaluation.

modules.title: Anatomy of an agent
modules.description: What separates an agent from a workflow, the loop at its core, its tools and protocol, and what it remembers.

modules.title: Architecture patterns
modules.description: Planning, composed workflows and multiple agents, and the costs each pattern carries.

modules.title: Governing agents
modules.description: Permissions, injection, traces, evaluation and human oversight: the controls that decide whether an agent can be trusted with a task.

concepts.title: Workflow
concepts.summary: Model calls and tools orchestrated by code along predefined paths.

concepts.title: Agent
concepts.summary: A system in which the model decides its own next steps and tool use within a loop.

concepts.title: Autonomy ladder
concepts.summary: Script, model-assisted workflow, copilot, agent: more freedom, less predictability.

concepts.title: Agent loop
concepts.summary: Repeat: model sees context, picks an action, the result is appended, until a stop condition holds.

concepts.title: Step budget
concepts.summary: A hard limit on iterations, tokens or time.

concepts.title: Compounding error
concepts.summary: Per-step reliability multiplies across steps.

concepts.title: Tool description
concepts.summary: The name, purpose, parameters and limits that the model reads when choosing a tool.

concepts.title: Read versus write tool
concepts.summary: A read tool only fetches; a write tool changes state.

concepts.title: Idempotency key
concepts.summary: A caller-supplied token so a repeated request has the effect of one.

concepts.title: Model Context Protocol
concepts.summary: An open protocol by which a client application discovers and calls tools, resources and prompts on a server.

concepts.title: JSON-RPC
concepts.summary: A message format of method, parameters and id, with a matching result or error.

concepts.title: Transport
concepts.summary: The channel carrying messages: standard input/output for local servers, HTTP for remote ones.

concepts.title: Working context
concepts.summary: What is in the prompt on this step.

concepts.title: Compaction
concepts.summary: Summarising old turns to free room.

concepts.title: External memory
concepts.summary: Notes and files the agent writes and reads back by tool.

concepts.title: Reason-act loop
concepts.summary: Interleave a short reasoning step with an action and an observation.

concepts.title: Plan then execute
concepts.summary: Write the whole plan first, then carry out steps, replanning on failure.

concepts.title: Reflection
concepts.summary: Critique the result or failure and retry with the critique.

concepts.title: Prompt chaining
concepts.summary: A fixed sequence of model calls, each taking the previous output.

concepts.title: Parallelisation
concepts.summary: Independent subtasks run at once (sectioning) or the same task run several times (voting).

concepts.title: Evaluator-optimiser
concepts.summary: One call proposes, another critiques, and the loop repeats until accepted.

concepts.title: Handoff
concepts.summary: One agent passing control and context to another.

concepts.title: Context isolation
concepts.summary: Giving a subagent only the context its task needs.

concepts.title: Agent contract
concepts.summary: The defined inputs, outputs and permissions between two agents.

concepts.title: Least privilege
concepts.summary: Giving an agent only the access its task needs.

concepts.title: Approval gate
concepts.summary: A human decision required before a risky action runs.

concepts.title: Audit log
concepts.summary: An append-only record of each action with who, what and why.

concepts.title: Lethal trifecta
concepts.summary: Access to private data, exposure to untrusted content and a way to communicate externally, in one agent.

concepts.title: Untrusted content
concepts.summary: Any text the agent reads that an attacker could have written.

concepts.title: Privilege separation
concepts.summary: Splitting work so that the part reading untrusted content has no powerful tools.

concepts.title: Trace
concepts.summary: The record of one run as nested spans for model calls, retrievals and tool calls.

concepts.title: 95th percentile
concepts.summary: The value below which 95% of observations fall (nearest rank: the ceil(0.95·n)th smallest).

concepts.title: Cost per success
concepts.summary: Total spend divided by the number of successful tasks.

concepts.title: Trajectory
concepts.summary: The sequence of actions an agent took, not only its final answer.

concepts.title: pass@k
concepts.summary: The chance that at least one of k attempts succeeds.

concepts.title: pass^k
concepts.summary: The chance that all k attempts succeed.

concepts.title: Oversight point
concepts.summary: Where a person approves, samples or can stop the agent.

concepts.title: Staged rollout
concepts.summary: Shadow, assist, then act, each gated by evidence.

concepts.title: Autonomy decision record
concepts.summary: A written decision stating the autonomy level, why, and the trigger for changing it.

lessons.title: Workflow, copilot or agent

lead.text: Return to the refund request. Suppose the system always classifies the message, looks up the order, checks the policy and writes a reply, in that order, with a language model doing the classifying, the policy check and the writing. The model is called three times, yet it never decides what happens next, because the order was fixed in code before the request arrived. In its guide to building effective agents, Anthropic's engineering team calls a system of this kind a **workflow**: language models and tools orchestrated through predefined code paths.

Now suppose the same system is given only the customer's message and a set of tools it may call. The model chooses a tool, receives the result, chooses again, and stops when it judges that the request has been dealt with. The guide calls this an **agent**: a system in which the model directs its own process and its use of tools, within a loop. The definition sits close to the one in Russell and Norvig's *Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach*, where an agent is anything that perceives its environment and acts on it, with the added condition that here the model is the part that chooses the action.

The difference therefore comes down to one question, **who decides the next step**. The number of model calls does not settle it, since a workflow may call a model ten times and an agent only once, and the presence of tools does not settle it either, since a workflow may call a tool at every step.

reveal.text: The code fixed the order before the transcript arrived, so the design is a workflow however many model calls it makes. A sixth call added to the sequence would not change that.

steps.headline: The ladder from script to agent

lead.text: The workflow and the agent are two points on a scale, and it helps to name its other rungs. At the bottom is the **script**, ordinary code in which no model chooses anything. Above it is the workflow, in which code still fixes the order but a model does work inside some of the steps. Next comes the **copilot**, in which the model proposes the next step and a person approves, edits or rejects it before anything happens. At the top is the agent, in which the model chooses the step and the tool with no person in between. Together the four rungs form the **autonomy ladder**.

afterFigure.text: Moving up a rung hands one more decision to the model, which is where the flexibility comes from. The same move removes something, because code can be tested on every input it will see and a model's choices cannot, so each rung up is *less predictable* than the one below it. The buttons in the figure show where the decision sits on each rung.

diagram.alt: A line of four rungs from script to agent. Each case highlights one rung and says who decides the next step: code for a script, code for the order in a workflow, a person approving the model in a copilot, and the model in an agent.
diagram.caption: The decision moves from code to the model as you climb. Use the buttons to move between rungs.

reveal.text: The agent costs $0.12 per request against $0.03, which is four times as much. The ratio equals the ratio of calls because the price per call is the same.

lead.text: The agent in the last question cost four times as much, and cost is one of several things that change as you climb. An agent's **latency**, the time a customer waits for the reply, grows with the number of calls and varies from one request to the next, whereas a workflow takes almost the same time on every request. Correctness moves in both directions: an agent can handle requests that the workflow's branches never anticipated, and it can also wander into the wrong tool. Auditability, the ability to say afterwards why something happened, is highest for a script, where the code is the explanation, and lowest for an agent.

afterFigure.text: When the refund policy is fixed and the only hard part is reading free text, a workflow meets the need, and the agent meets it too but at four times the cost. When every dispute needs a different investigation and there are too many for a person to handle, only the agent meets the need. The rule that follows is to choose **the lowest rung that meets the need**, and to say in advance what evidence would justify climbing.

steps.headline: Choose the rung for the standard refund process, then price it for a month.

workedSteps.text: List the steps the process needs: classify the message, look up the order, check the 30-day refund policy, and write the reply.
Ask whether the order of the steps ever depends on what an earlier step returns. Here it does not, because every request needs the same four steps in the same order.
A fixed order means code can hold the path, so the lowest rung that meets the need is a workflow. The lookup is plain code, and the other three steps are model calls.
Price one request at $0.01 for each model call.
A month brings 1,000 requests, and each one costs the same.

lead.text: A team proposes an agent to answer the question "Where is my order?". Every such answer comes from one order lookup followed by one templated sentence, and no request has ever needed anything else.

reveal.text: Where the steps never vary there is nothing for a model to decide, so the cheapest design that meets the need is also the most predictable one.

lead.text: A design that records its rung should also record a **trigger**, a measurable condition under which the next rung becomes worth its cost, such as the share of requests that the fixed path cannot resolve. Suppose the refund workflow resolves 94 requests in every 100 and the other 6 reach a person. Sending all 100 through an agent would multiply the cost of the 94 that the workflow already handles, whereas sending only the 6 to an agent pays the higher price on just the requests that need it.
A router that makes that split is itself a workflow, so different parts of one product can sit on different rungs, each at the lowest rung that meets its own need.

A router sends 6% of the 2,000 refund requests a day straight to the agent, which costs $0.12 per request, and the rest through the workflow, which costs $0.03 per request. Ignore the router's own cost.

reveal.text: Most of the bill still comes from the workflow's 1,880 requests, but the agent's 120 requests add up to about a fifth of the total, so the trigger that sends requests to the agent also controls the budget.

lessons.orientation: Place a refund process on the autonomy ladder and choose the lowest rung that meets the need.
lessons.nextAction: Follow the agent loop step by step and see what stops it and how errors compound.

blocks.text: A customer writes that an order arrived damaged and asks for the money back. To deal with it, a support system has to decide what kind of message this is, find the order, check the refund policy and send a reply, and there is more than one way to build that. In one design, ordinary code runs the four steps in a fixed order and calls a language model to classify the message, check the policy and write the reply. In another, the model is given tools such as an order lookup and a refund button, and left to decide which to use and when to stop.

Both designs answer the customer, but they differ in who decides what happens next. That one difference changes what the system costs, how long the customer waits and how easily anyone can explain afterwards what it did, and it is the basis for deciding how much freedom a model should be given for any particular task.

diagram.alt: The same refund request handled two ways. In the first, code runs classify, look up order, check policy and write reply in a fixed order. In the second, a model repeatedly chooses among four tools.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to place a process on the ladder from script to agent, compare the cost of two designs, and choose the lowest rung that meets the need.
intro.whyItMatters: Autonomy is bought with cost, delay and predictability, so a design should not pay for more than the task needs.

recap.keyIdea: The autonomy ladder runs from script to workflow to copilot to agent, and the lowest rung that meets the need is the right one, because each rung up costs predictability, money and time.

blocks.text: A workflow lets code fix the path and an agent lets the model choose it, so the test is who decides the next step, whatever the number of model calls. Each rung up the ladder hands the model more of the decisions, and the gap between a three-call workflow and a twelve-call agent, four to one in cost, shows the price of that freedom. A design should therefore start at the lowest rung that meets the need and name the measurement that would justify climbing.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson follows the agent rung in detail, tracing its loop step by step and showing what stops it.

lessons.title: The agent loop

lead.text: At each step of an agent's run, the model is given the **context**, which holds the goal and everything that has happened since, and it replies with an action: usually a call to one of its tools. The code around the model carries out that call and appends the result, called the **observation**, to the context, and the model is then called again with the longer context. This cycle is the **agent loop**, and it is the whole mechanism, since everything an agent appears to do is some number of passes through it.

The figure follows one run for the refund goal from the last lesson. In step 3 the model replies with a sentence and no tool call, and that absence is what ends the run. The pattern is the one that Yao and colleagues described in the ReAct paper, in which a model alternates between reasoning and acting and reads each result before choosing the next step.

diagram.alt: Three stages of one agent run. The context starts with a goal about order 4471. After step 1 it holds a lookup call and its result, after step 2 a policy check and its result, and after step 3 the final answer, which has no tool call and ends the run.

reveal.text: The model was called once per pass, and the fifth pass produced the answer, so the loop made five model calls and four tool calls. The final answer is the model's output of a pass like any other.
The model's own judgement that it is finished cannot be relied on, so the code needs a limit that does not depend on it. The next screen sets out the ways a loop can end.

lead.text: The loop in the last figure ended because the model wrote an answer, which is the way a well-behaved run finishes, but it is only one of four. A run can also end on an error that the code treats as fatal, or on a request from a person who watches the run and cancels it. The fourth is a **step budget**: a hard limit on the number of iterations, or on tokens or time, after which the code ends the loop whatever the model has chosen.

The first three depend on something outside the code behaving as hoped, and only the budget is enforced by the loop itself. The program in the figure has no answer to wait for, and it still ends when the step reaches the budget of 4, because the condition "`step < budget`" is then false.

diagram.code:
step = 0
budget = 4
while step < budget:
    step = step + 1

lead.text: The model keeps no memory between calls, which is why the code sends the context afresh each time, with the new call and result appended. The input to step 1 is the starting context, say 1,000 [[tokens|Chunks of text a model reads or writes. Met in AI Engineering.]], and each step then adds 400 tokens, so the input to step 2 is 1,400 tokens, the input to step 3 is 1,800, and so on. Every call is billed on its whole input, and although a provider's prompt caching can charge the repeated part at a lower rate, this lesson counts every token at the full rate, so the cost of a run is the *sum* of these inputs, not the size of the last one.

The trace in the figure adds up the inputs of the first four steps: 1,000 + 1,400 + 1,800 + 2,200, which comes to 6,400. A run twice as long costs more than twice as much, because each added step is more expensive than the one before it.

diagram.code:
tokens = 1000
total = 0
step = 1
while step <= 4:
    total = total + tokens
    tokens = tokens + 400
    step = step + 1

reveal.text: Ten steps read 1,000, 1,400 and so on up to 4,600 tokens, which adds to 28,000 and not 10,000. The last step alone costs 4.6 times the first, which is why long runs are expensive.
The three steps all have to succeed, so the chances multiply: 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 = 0.729. A run of three steps that are each 90% reliable succeeds only about 73% of the time.

lead.text: Three steps that each succeed 90% of the time all succeed with probability 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 = 0.729, and the same arithmetic holds for any run. If each step succeeds with probability p, the steps are independent, and the task needs every one of n steps to succeed, then the chance of finishing is p multiplied by itself n times, written pⁿ. This is **compounding error**: a small chance of failure at each step, repeated, adds up to a large chance of failure over the run. It also means that the usual reading of a per-step figure is too generous, since a step that is right 95% of the time sounds dependable, and a ten-step task built from such steps is dependable only *about 60% of the time*.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows the same 95% step in tasks of 5, 10 and 20 steps, which finish with probabilities of about 77%, 60% and 36%. The assumptions behind the numbers matter: real steps are not always independent, and a good agent can sometimes notice a failed step and retry it. Even so, the calculation gives the right instinct, that each step added to a run has a price in reliability, and that shortening a run can raise reliability more than improving each step slightly.

steps.headline: Find the chance that a 20-step run succeeds when each step succeeds 98% of the time.

workedSteps.text: All 20 steps must succeed, and the steps are independent, so the chance is 0.98 multiplied by itself 20 times, which a calculator takes as a single power.
The calculator shows a long decimal, and the answer is wanted to two places.

lead.text: A team improves its agent so that each step succeeds 99% of the time instead of 95%. The task is still ten steps long, and the steps are independent.

reveal.text: The run now finishes about 90% of the time, against about 60% before, so a four-point gain per step became a thirty-point gain over the run.

lead.text: A team sets a step budget of 8 for a run whose input is 1,000 tokens at step 1 and grows by 400 tokens at each later step. They want the most input the loop can ever read.

reveal.text: Because the budget caps the number of steps, it also caps the input, so the worst case is known before the run starts. The ceiling is a figure the team can price, which an unbounded loop cannot offer.

lessons.orientation: Trace an agent loop, set the limit that ends it, and work out what a run costs and how often it succeeds.
lessons.nextAction: Design the tools an agent calls, so that the loop has something useful to choose between.

blocks.text: A single call to a language model sends a prompt and receives text. An agent makes many calls, and each call carries the original request together with everything that has happened since, which is the model's earlier choices and the results they produced, so every call is longer than the one before.

That growth is one reason an agent's run has to be bounded, and reliability is another, because a step that works 95 times in 100 sounds dependable, yet ten such steps in a row all succeed only about 60 times in 100. Both effects depend on how many times the loop goes round, so once you know how the loop works you can predict what a run will cost and how often it will finish, and decide where the code around the model has to stop it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to trace a run of the loop, add a stop condition and a step budget, and compute how cost and reliability change as a run lengthens.
intro.whyItMatters: Cost and reliability both depend on how many steps a run takes, and the code around the model has to bound that number.

recap.keyIdea: An agent loop repeats until a stop condition holds, and because each step re-reads a growing context and multiplies in a chance of failure, a step budget is what keeps cost and reliability in bounds.

blocks.text: The model sees the context, chooses an action, and the result is appended to the context before the model is called again, so the input grows by one call and one result at every step. A run ends when the model answers, when an error is fatal, when a person cancels it or when the step budget is reached, and only the last of these is certain to happen. Because per-step success rates multiply, a long run is much less reliable than any one of its steps, which makes a short run with a firm limit worth more than a long one that depends on the model deciding to stop.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson takes up the tools themselves: what a good tool description contains, and how a tool that changes things should be built.

lessons.title: Designing tools

lead.text: The model never sees a tool's code. What it receives is a **tool description**: the tool's name, a passage saying what it does, and a schema listing its parameters with their types. It chooses between tools by reading these, in just the way it reads a prompt, which makes a tool description part of the prompt and deserving of the same care. Anthropic's guide to building agents makes the same point about what it calls the agent-computer interface, saying that a team should put as much effort into the design of its tools as into the design of its prompts.

A description that does this work says what the tool does, when to use it and when not to, what each input means and in what form, and what comes back. The vague version in the figure leaves the model to guess at all of these, whereas the precise version tells it, for instance, that the order identifier comes from an earlier tool and that the amount may not exceed the order total. The *name* matters less than people expect, because two tools called `lookup` and `find` with the same thin description are indistinguishable to the model however well they are named.

diagram.alt: The same refund tool described two ways. The vague description says only that it refunds a customer. The precise one says what it does, when to use it and when not to, what each input means, and what it returns.
diagram.caption: The model reads these words to choose and call the tool. Use the buttons to compare the two descriptions.

reveal.text: The precise version says when to send, where the address comes from and what is returned, which is what the model cannot find out by trying. The other two leave those points to a guess, and the last one invites a retry that could send the same email twice.

lead.text: The tools `search_orders`, `get_customer` and `read_policy` only *fetch*: after any number of calls the shop is exactly as it was, which is why they are called **read tools**. The tools `issue_refund` and `send_email` leave something behind, since money has left the shop and a message has reached a customer, and a tool of that kind is a **write tool**. Anything that creates, changes, deletes, sends or pays is a write tool, whatever its name suggests.

afterFigure.text: The distinction matters because the cost of a wrong call is so different. A wrong read costs a call and a little context, whereas an email cannot be unsent, and a refund that was not due has to be recovered by other means. OWASP's 2025 list of risks for applications built on language models names *excessive agency*, giving a model tools that can do more than its task requires, as one of them.

reveal.text: Ending a plan changes what the customer is charged, and it cannot be seen as a fetch, so the tool is a write tool however gentle its name sounds.

lead.text: What a tool returns when it fails is read by the model in the same way as everything else in its context. An error that says only "400" leaves the model to guess, and a model that guesses often repeats the same call. An error that says "amount 5000 is more than the order total of 3800 cents; retry with an amount of at most 3800" gives the model the fact it lacked and the action to take.

The better remedy is sometimes to make the mistake impossible. Anthropic's guide describes a coding agent whose tools took relative file paths, and which made errors with them once it had moved out of the root directory; the team changed the tool so that it required absolute paths, and the errors stopped.

reveal.text: Each call that reached the server paid out, so the customer has been refunded three times. The agent was right to retry, since it could not know that the first call had succeeded, and the fault lies in a tool that cannot tell a retry from a new request.

lead.text: The agent in the last example cannot avoid retrying, because after a timeout it has no way to tell whether the request never arrived or its reply was lost. The remedy is to make the write safe to repeat. An operation is **idempotent** if doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once, and a write is made idempotent with an **idempotency key**: a token chosen by the caller for one intended action and sent with every attempt at it. The server stores each key with the result of the first request that used it, and a later request with the same key receives that stored result without a second refund being made.

The key identifies the *action*, not the attempt. The caller makes one for each refund it intends and reuses it on every retry of that refund, so that three attempts at one refund make one refund; a different refund gets a different key.

diagram.alt: Two cases of an agent sending the same refund request three times after timeouts. Without an idempotency key the server makes three refunds. With the same key on every call the server makes one refund and returns the stored result to the later calls.
diagram.caption: The agent cannot know whether its first call arrived, so it retries. Use the buttons to compare the two servers.

steps.headline: Count how many refunds the server makes when five calls arrive with these keys, in this order: a, a, b, a, b.

workedSteps.text: The server starts with no keys stored. The first call carries key a, which it has not seen, so it makes a refund and stores a with the result.
The second call also carries a. The key is stored, so the server returns the stored result and makes no refund.
The third call carries b, a key the server has not seen before.
The fourth call repeats a and the fifth repeats b, and the server checks each one against the keys it has stored.
The server has now handled all five calls.

lead.text: A team builds the key for each refund from the order number alone, so that every call about order 4471 carries the key `refund-4471`. A customer is owed two partial refunds on that order, $10 and then $15, and the agent makes the two calls on different days.

reveal.text: The server found a stored key on the second call and returned the first refund's result, so the customer received $10 and never the $15. A key must identify the intended action, which here means the refund, and an order can have more than one.

lessons.orientation: Classify tools as read or write, write a description the model can use, and make a write tool safe to retry.
lessons.nextAction: Meet the protocol that lets one agent use tools from many servers.

blocks.text: A support agent has five tools: it can search orders, fetch a customer record, read the refund policy, issue a refund and send an email. The model never sees the code behind any of them. For each tool it receives a name, a description and a list of typed parameters, and everything it does with the tool follows from reading those few lines.

That makes the description the place where most mistakes either start or are prevented, since a model that misreads one will call the wrong tool, or pass the wrong input, with complete confidence. The tools that change things outside the conversation raise a second problem, which is what the agent should do when it calls one and never hears back, and the design of the tool decides whether the agent can then safely try again.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to classify a tool as read or write, judge whether a description is usable, and explain how an idempotency key makes a retried write safe.
intro.whyItMatters: Tools are the only way an agent acts, so their descriptions and their behaviour on retry decide whether a run is safe.

recap.keyIdea: A tool is the model's only view of an action, so its description has to be precise, its writes have to be told apart from its reads, and every write has to be safe to retry.

blocks.text: The model chooses and calls tools by reading their descriptions and their error messages, which are therefore part of the prompt and need the same care. A read tool changes nothing and can be called again at will, whereas a write tool leaves an effect that cannot be taken back. Because a reply can be lost after a write has succeeded, a write is given an idempotency key chosen for one intended action, so that three attempts at the action make one change.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at the protocol that lets an agent discover and call tools offered by other programs, and at how agents talk to each other.

lessons.title: Tool protocols: MCP and agent-to-agent

steps.headline: One protocol instead of many links

lead.text: If there are N applications and M tools, and each application is wired directly to each tool, that is N × M integrations. The **Model Context Protocol**, or **MCP**, which Anthropic introduced in November 2024 as an open specification, replaces those integrations with one agreed message format: an application implements the client side once, a tool provider implements the server side once, and any client can then use any server, so the work comes to N + M implementations.
MCP is therefore a wire protocol, a specification of the messages that two programs exchange, and it is not a framework for building agents.

reveal.text: Wired directly, the seventh tool needs four new integrations, one for each application. With a shared protocol it needs one implementation, which is why the gap widens as either number grows.

lead.text: The protocol names three parts. The **host** is the application the user is working in, and it contains the model. Inside the host, a **client** holds a connection to one server and speaks the protocol on the host's behalf. The **server** is the program that offers tools, and it does two things: it describes the tools it has, and it runs one when asked.

The second view of the figure shows who decides what, which is where a common misunderstanding arises. The model, which is in the host, reads the tool descriptions and chooses a tool; the client sends the call; and the server runs the tool and returns what it produced. A server does not choose which of its tools the model uses, any more than a shop chooses what a customer buys. It tells the host what exists and carries out what it is told.

diagram.alt: A host application on the left holding a model and a client, and a server on the right with three tools, joined by JSON-RPC messages. The second view marks who does what: the model chooses a tool, the client sends the call, and the server runs the tool.
diagram.caption: The host owns the model and the choice; the server describes tools and runs them. Use the buttons to switch views.

reveal.text: The email server runs the tool, and the host only receives its result. This split is what lets a tool be written once and used by any application that speaks the protocol.

lead.text: MCP's messages are written in **JSON-RPC** 2.0, a small standard for calling a named operation on another program. A request has four members. The `jsonrpc` member gives the version, `method` names the operation, `params` holds its inputs, and `id` is a number or string chosen by the sender. The reply carries the same `id`, and it holds either a result or an error, never both.

afterFigure.text: A tool that ran and failed also returns a result, with `isError` set to `true`, so that the model can read the error message, whereas a request the server cannot understand at all comes back as a JSON-RPC error. A message with no `id` is a notification, to which no reply is made.

diagram.alt: A JSON-RPC request and its response. The request carries jsonrpc 2.0, id 7, the method tools/call and params naming the tool search_orders with the argument customer c-42. The response carries the same id 7 and a result holding the tool's text.
diagram.caption: Notes beside each line say what the field is for. Use the buttons to move between request and response.

steps.headline: A session from start to call

lead.text: A connection starts with a short exchange in which each side states what it can do. The client sends an `initialize` request giving the protocol version it supports and its capabilities, and the server answers with its own version and capabilities, which include whether it offers tools. The client then sends a notification that it is ready. Only after this exchange does the client send `tools/list`, whose result is the list of tools, each with a name, a description and a schema for its inputs, and these are exactly the descriptions the model reads when it chooses.
The third phase is the one the agent loop uses, and it repeats: each time the model chooses a tool, the client sends a `tools/call` and waits for the result.

diagram.alt: A sequence diagram of an MCP session between a client and a server. The client sends initialize and the server answers, the client sends an initialized notification, then asks tools/list and receives the list, and finally sends tools/call and receives the result. Each view highlights one phase.
diagram.caption: Messages flow between client and server in a fixed order. Use the buttons to move through the three phases.

reveal.text: MCP defines two transports, the channels that carry its messages. For a local server the host starts the program and exchanges messages over its **standard input and output**, known as stdio. A remote server is reached over HTTP, in the form the specification calls Streamable HTTP, so that one server can serve many clients on other machines.

steps.headline: Match the reply to the request, then read what it says.

workedSteps.text: The client has three `tools/call` requests waiting: `id` 12 for `search_orders` with the customer `c-42`, `id` 13 for `read_policy`, and `id` 14 for `get_customer`.
A reply arrives that carries `id` 12. Replies do not always come back in the order the requests were sent, so the client has to work out which request this one answers.
Inside `result`, the `content` holds the text `"orders 4471, 4502"`, and `isError` is `false`, so the tool ran and found two orders.

reveal.text: The shared protocol needs 6 + 9 = 15 implementations against 6 × 9 = 54 bespoke integrations. Each new tool server then costs one implementation, where before it cost six.

lead.text: MCP is built for the case where the other side is a *tool server*: it lists tools, runs them and returns results, and it has no goals of its own. Agents also need to work with other agents, and that is a different problem, since the other party plans and decides for itself. The Agent2Agent protocol, written A2A, is designed for it: an agent publishes a description of what it can do, often called an agent card, and another agent can discover it, send it a task and follow the task's status until a result comes back.
The two protocols are complementary and one product can use both: an agent may use MCP for its own tools and A2A to hand a task to another agent.

diagram.alt: Two protocols compared. In MCP an agent host connects to tool servers such as order tools, email tools and policy files. In A2A one agent, a shop agent, sends a task to another agent, a courier agent run by another company, and receives its status and result.
diagram.caption: MCP connects an agent to tools and data; A2A connects an agent to another agent. Use the buttons to compare.

lead.text: A travel agent has to look up flight times in an airline's timetable system, which returns data only when asked. It also has to hand the booking of a hotel room to the hotel chain's own agent, which checks availability and negotiates the price by itself and may answer the next day.

reveal.text: The hotel chain's agent plans and decides for itself, so handing it a task is the case A2A was designed for. The timetable system is a tool, which MCP serves.

lessons.orientation: Read a JSON-RPC tool request and say which side owns each part of the Model Context Protocol.
lessons.nextAction: Manage what an agent keeps in its context as a run grows.

blocks.text: Suppose three applications each need to use five tools. If every application is wired directly to every tool, someone writes and maintains 15 separate integrations, and a sixth tool adds another three and a fourth application another five. The work grows as a product, and it is repeated by every team that builds an agent.

A shared protocol changes the arithmetic, since each application and each tool then has to speak the protocol only once, which makes 3 + 5 = 8 pieces of work, and a sixth tool adds one more piece instead of three. The Model Context Protocol is such a protocol for agents and their tools, and reading its messages is how you can tell what a tool server offers an agent and what the agent asked it to do.

diagram.alt: Two wirings of three applications and five tools. Without a protocol every application is connected directly to every tool, 15 connections. With a shared protocol each application and each tool connects only to the protocol, 8 connections.
diagram.caption: Use the buttons to compare direct wiring with a shared protocol.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to read a JSON-RPC tool request, say which side owns each part of MCP, and tell MCP apart from an agent-to-agent protocol.
intro.whyItMatters: Most real agents reach their tools through a protocol, so reading its messages is how you tell what an agent can do and what it did.

recap.keyIdea: MCP is a wire protocol in which a host's client discovers and calls the tools of a server through JSON-RPC messages, and the model, not the server, chooses which tool to call.

blocks.text: A host contains the model, a client holds one connection to one server, and the server describes its tools and runs them. A request names its operation in `method`, carries inputs in `params` and is answered by a reply with the same `id`, and a session runs through initialisation, `tools/list` and then `tools/call`, over stdio for a local server or HTTP for a remote one. A2A is a different protocol, for an agent that hands work to another agent, so the two are used together and not instead of one another.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to what an agent keeps in its context as a run grows, and what it does when the context fills.

lessons.title: Memory and context management

lead.text: At each step the model reads a context that holds its instructions, the descriptions of its tools, the conversation so far and every tool result that has come back. These together are the **working context**, which is what is in the prompt on this step, and the **context window** is the most that a model can read in a single call. The second view adds a tool result of 21,000 tokens, which brings the total to 83,000 and past the dashed line at 80,000, the point at which this agent has been set to compact its context.

afterFigure.text: A larger window does not make the budget unnecessary. Every token in the context is read again at every step and paid for each time, as the cost arithmetic of the [[agent loop|The cycle in which the model chooses an action and the result is added to the context. Met in 'The agent loop'.]] showed, and a model may use information in a very long context less reliably than information in a short one.

reveal.text: The trigger is at 150,000 tokens, and the agent has used 120,000 of them. Any tool result larger than 30,000 tokens will therefore start compaction on its own.
The summary is twenty times smaller than what it replaces, so it can hold the gist of the history and only a fraction of its detail. The next screen shows how to choose what the summary keeps.

lead.text: **Compaction** replaces the older part of the context with a summary written by the model, and keeps the most recent turns word for word. In the figure it takes the 83,000 tokens in use down to 24,000: the 8,000 of instructions stay, the old turns and results become a summary of 4,000, and the latest 12,000 tokens are kept as they were. The agent then has room for many more steps before it needs to compact again.

What a summary drops is the price of the room it frees. A summary keeps the outline of what happened and tends to lose exact values, identifiers and the reasoning behind a decision, which may be the very detail that a later step needs, so the instruction to the summariser should say what to preserve: decisions made, identifiers such as an order number, values that were quoted, and tasks still open. Anthropic's account of its multi-agent research system describes the same practice, in which agents summarise completed phases of their work and store the essential information outside the context before they move on.

reveal.text: Compaction is chosen when old turns are no longer needed word for word, and it frees room at the cost of detail.

lead.text: Some facts cannot be left to a summary, because they have to be available exactly and in later runs as well as in this one. For these an agent has **external memory**: notes and files that it writes with one tool and reads back with another. External memory takes no room in the window until something is read from it, and it survives both compaction and the end of the run. What belongs there is what would be costly to lose: the decisions made, a user's standing preferences, the tasks still open, and the plan.

afterFigure.text: Memory differs from retrieval in one respect that matters for safety: retrieval only reads, whereas memory is also written, so a wrong note persists and is read as fact by every later run. A memory tool is a write tool in the sense of the earlier lesson.

reveal.text: A preference that has to outlast the run cannot rely on the context or on a summary, so the agent writes it to the store and reads it when it is relevant.

steps.headline: Work out whether a 15,000-token tool result sets off compaction when 71,000 tokens of the 100,000-token window are in use.

workedSteps.text: The agent compacts at 80% of the window, so the trigger is at 80% of 100,000 tokens.
The history before the result is 71,000 tokens. Adding the result of 15,000 tokens gives the new total.
Compare the total with the trigger: 86,000 is above 80,000, so compaction runs, although 14,000 tokens of the window are still free.

steps.headline: Work out whether a result of 8,000 tokens triggers compaction in a 128,000-token window set to compact at 75%, with 90,000 tokens in use.

workedSteps.text: Find the trigger: 75% of the window.
The history is 90,000 tokens, and the result adds 8,000 tokens to it.
The total is above 96,000, so compaction runs.

reveal.text: The larger window moves the trigger out to 160,000 tokens and puts the total, 83,000, far below it, so compaction is postponed. The postponed steps are not free, because each one re-reads the larger context, which is why a bigger window delays the problem and leaves the planning in place.

lead.text: On Monday the agent wrote this note to external memory: "Refund for order 4502 approved." On Tuesday the refund was refused after review, and nobody updated the note. On Wednesday a new session starts and reads its notes.

reveal.text: The agent has no way to know that the note is stale, so it treats the note as true. The fix lies in the write tools: a note needs an owner, a date and a way to be corrected.

lessons.orientation: Decide what an agent keeps in its context, summarises or stores outside it, and compute when compaction triggers.
lessons.nextAction: Compare the planning patterns that decide what an agent does with its steps.

blocks.text: An agent that has been running for an hour holds, in its context, every instruction it was given, the description of every tool, each turn of the conversation and every result that came back. If the window is 100,000 tokens and 62,000 are already in use, a single tool result of 21,000 tokens takes the total to 83,000, which is past the 80,000 at which this agent has been set to make room, and the agent has either to throw something away or to stop. Which things to throw away, which to shorten and which to keep somewhere else is a design decision, and it is made before the run starts.
Getting that decision right is what lets an agent keep working for hours without losing what it was told at the start.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to decide what an agent keeps in context, summarises or stores outside it, and compute the point at which compaction triggers.
intro.whyItMatters: An agent that runs long must plan its context, because the window limits what it can see and every token in it is paid for again at each step.

recap.keyIdea: An agent plans its context as a budget: it keeps what the current step needs, compacts what is old, and writes what must last to external memory.

blocks.text: The working context is a budget of tokens, and compaction is triggered when use passes a set share of the window, as a tool result of 21,000 tokens does when 62,000 are already in use in a window of 100,000. A summary frees room by losing detail, so what must survive exactly, such as decisions, preferences and open tasks, is written to external memory, where a wrong note persists and has to be treated like any other write. A bigger window postpones these decisions without removing them.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at planning patterns, the ways an agent can organise its steps before and while it takes them.

lessons.title: Planning and reasoning patterns

lead.text: A nightly export job has failed, and nobody yet knows why. The first thing to do is to read its log, and what to do second depends on what the log says, so no one could write the steps in advance. The **reason-act loop** meets this by interleaving a short reasoning step with an action and its observation: the model writes a line of reasoning, takes one action, reads the result, and reasons again with the result in front of it. Yao and colleagues introduced the pattern, called ReAct, in a 2022 paper.

afterFigure.text: After the log shows a full disk, the agent's next line of reasoning asks which folder is largest, and that question exists only because of what the log said. A reason-act loop therefore adapts at every step, and pays for it with one model call per step. The reasoning lines help a person follow the run, but they are not a verified account of how the model reached its answer.

diagram.alt: Three stages of a reason-act run investigating a failing nightly job. After the first step the agent has read the log and seen a disk-full error. After the second it has measured disk usage and found 41 GB of 50 GB in /data/tmp. After the third it reasons that temporary files are the cause and plans to ask before clearing them.
diagram.caption: Each reasoning step depends on the last observation. Use the buttons to follow the run.

reveal.text: The steps cannot be written until the first result is read, so the decision has to be made again after each observation, which is what the reason-act loop does.

The plan-then-execute agent makes three calls against the loop's eight, so planning first is much cheaper here. Two things limit the saving: it holds only while the plan survives, and every replan is another model call.

lead.text: Some tasks have steps that are known before the first action. Filing an expense claim means opening the form, entering the claimant and the amount, attaching the receipt, submitting and saving the confirmation, and none of that depends on what any step returns. For a task of this kind the agent can write the whole plan first and then carry it out, which is **plan then execute**.

afterFigure.text: A plan is a guess about the future, and an observation can break it. In the figure the receipt is too large to attach at step 4, so the agent keeps the three steps already done, notes the failed attempt, and writes a new plan from step 4 onwards, so 3 steps done, 1 failed and 3 new make 7 actions in all. Plan then execute therefore works best when the steps are predictable and a failure is rare.

diagram.alt: A six-step expense-claim plan and what happens when step 4, attaching the receipt, fails. Steps 1 to 3 are done, step 4 fails because the file is too large, and a new three-step plan replaces the rest: shrink the receipt, attach it and submit, save the confirmation. In all, 7 actions are taken.
diagram.caption: A plan is cheap to follow until an observation breaks it. Use the buttons to see the failure and the new plan.

class="t-small" x="577.0" y="127.0" text-anchor="middle">confirmation</text><text class="t-small t-muted" x="525" y="164" text-anchor="middle">dropped</text></svg>

reveal.text: The plan is written first and four steps succeed. The failure at step 5 is one wasted action, and the new plan is one more model call, which is why replanning has a price.

lead.text: The third pattern acts on a result that has already been produced. In **reflection** the agent checks an attempt, writes a short critique of what was wrong, and tries again with the critique in its context. Shinn and colleagues describe the method in the Reflexion paper, in which an agent turns feedback from a task, such as the failures reported by unit tests, into written reflections that it keeps for the next attempt, and they report that a coding agent built this way solved 91% of the HumanEval benchmark's coding problems on the first try at a time when GPT-4 without it was reported at 80%.

afterFigure.text: The word that matters in that account is *feedback*. In the figure's first view the tests report that 2 of 20 fail, and the critique can name the cause because the test supplied it. In the second view the model is asked whether its answer is right, and it replies that it thinks so, which gives it nothing new to act on, so another attempt will probably repeat the first. Reflection is therefore only as good as its signal: a test result, a checker or a measurement is reliable, and the model's own confidence is not.

diagram.alt: Two reflection loops. With a test as the signal, the tests report 2 of 20 failing, the critique names the cause, rounding applied before tax, and the next attempt can fix it. With only the model's own opinion, the model says it thinks the answer is right and nothing new is learned.
diagram.caption: Reflection improves an answer when a check supplies a fact. Use the buttons to compare the two.

reveal.text: The compiler gave the agent an outside measure of the fault, so it could aim the second attempt at it and see that the attempt had worked without trusting its own opinion.

steps.headline: Choose a pattern for setting up a new employee's accounts, using three questions about the task.

workedSteps.text: Are the steps known before the first action? Create the account, add it to the right groups, enrol the employee in payroll and send the welcome email: they are, and none of them depends on what another returns.
Might an observation change the task? Occasionally, as when the chosen user name is already taken, but then only the tail of the plan changes.
Is there a check that supplies a fact? Each system reports success or an error, so a failure is visible without the model's opinion.
These three answers point to one of the three patterns.

lead.text: The plan-then-execute agent from the cost question makes one call for the plan and uses the model in two steps. This time a step fails, so it makes one more call to write a new plan, and the new plan again uses the model in two steps.

reveal.text: The agent makes six calls against the loop's eight, so most of the saving has gone. A task that fails often would lose the rest, which is the sense in which a rigid plan stops being cheaper.

lead.text: A reviewer reads a reason-act run and finds that every reasoning line looks sensible and that the final answer follows from them. The agent proposed deleting old files from a shared drive.

reveal.text: Sensible-looking reasoning is text, and a fluent account can accompany a wrong action. Before a deletion the useful evidence comes from outside the model: a listing of the files, or an approval from a person.

lessons.orientation: Choose between acting step by step, planning first and reflecting, for a given task.
lessons.nextAction: Combine model calls into chains, parallel branches and evaluator loops.

blocks.text: Three tasks can be handed to the same agent with the same tools. To fix a nightly export job that has failed, the agent must read the log before it can know what to do next, whereas to file an expense claim it can list every step before it starts, and to write code that passes a test suite it can try, read the failures and try again. The tasks differ in what the agent knows at the start and in whether anything outside the model can tell it that a result is wrong.
Those two differences decide how the agent should organise its steps: choosing each one after seeing the last result, writing a plan first, or critiquing a finished attempt.

diagram.alt: Three flows an agent can follow. A reason-act loop alternates reasoning, acting and observing. Plan then execute writes a plan, follows its steps and writes a new plan if a step fails. Reflection makes an attempt, checks it, writes a critique and tries again.
diagram.caption: Each flow puts the decision in a different place. Use the buttons to compare the three.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to choose between a reason-act loop, plan then execute and reflection for a task, and count the actions or calls each takes.
intro.whyItMatters: The pattern an agent uses decides how many model calls it makes, how it recovers from a failure, and whether it can improve a result.

recap.keyIdea: Choose the reason-act loop when the steps depend on what is observed, plan then execute when the steps are known, and reflection when a check supplies a fact to learn from.

blocks.text: A reason-act loop decides each step after the last result and pays one model call for each, plan then execute writes the steps first and repairs them when an observation breaks the plan, and reflection critiques a finished attempt and retries. Planning first costs fewer calls only while the plan survives, since each replan adds a failed attempt and a new plan, and reflection helps only where a test or checker supplies a fact the model did not have. In every pattern the reasoning the model writes is text, and a sensible-looking line is not evidence that the step was right.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson combines model calls into fixed workflow patterns: chains, parallel branches and evaluator loops.

lessons.title: Composed workflow patterns

lead.text: Anthropic's guide to building agents describes five workflow patterns, which are ways of composing model calls in code so that the path stays under the programmer's control. The simplest is **prompt chaining**, a fixed sequence of calls in which each takes the output of the one before: an outline, then a draft written from the outline, then a translation of the draft.

**Routing** begins with a call that classifies the input and sends it to one of several specialised follow-ups, which suits a task that falls into distinct kinds, such as a support message that is about billing, shipping or a fault. In both patterns the structure is fixed before the input arrives.

reveal.text: The order never changes and each call reads only what the last one produced, which makes the design a chain. The programmer can test each link separately.
All three run together, so the work is finished when the slowest branch is. The figure on the next screen shows why the three times are not added.

lead.text: **Parallelisation** runs model calls that do not depend on one another at the same time. Anthropic's guide describes two forms: *sectioning*, in which a task is split into independent parts that run together, and *voting*, in which the same task is run several times to obtain several answers that are then compared. Branches of 4, 6 and 5 seconds run one after another take 4 + 6 + 5 = 15 seconds, and run at the same time they take only as long as the slowest, which is 6.

afterFigure.text: The time is the slowest branch *plus* any step that merges the results. And parallel branches save time and not money, because each branch is still a model call and all of them are paid for, so a parallel design is justified by latency or by the quality of the result, and not by cost.

diagram.alt: Two timelines for three branches taking 4, 6 and 5 seconds. Run one after another they take 4 + 6 + 5 = 15 seconds. Run at the same time they all finish when the slowest one, 6 seconds, finishes.
diagram.caption: The axis is in seconds. Use the buttons to compare running the branches in sequence and at once.

reveal.text: Run in sequence, the same work would take 7 + 3 + 9 + 2 = 21 seconds, so running the branches together saves 10 seconds, though the merge stays on the critical path.

lead.text: Voting runs the same task several times and takes the answer that most runs agree on. Suppose three independent voters are each right with probability *p*, and the majority wins. The majority is right if all three are right, which has probability p³, or if exactly two are, and there are three ways to choose which two, each with probability p² × (1 − p). The chance that the majority is right is therefore 3p²(1 − p) + p³.

For p = 0.8 this is 3 × 0.64 × 0.2 + 0.512 = 0.384 + 0.512 = 0.896, so the vote lifts an 80% voter to about 90%. The formula also shows when voting fails to help. At p = 0.5 the majority is right half the time, no better than one voter, and at p = 0.4 it falls to 0.352, *worse* than one voter. The calculation also assumes independence, and voters that are the same model with the same prompt tend to make the same mistakes, so the real gain is smaller than the formula suggests.

diagram.alt: Bars comparing one voter with a majority of three independent voters. With voters right 80 percent of the time the majority is right 0.896. At 50 percent the majority is right 0.5. At 40 percent it falls to 0.352, worse than one voter.

steps.headline: Find the chance that a majority of three independent voters is right when each is right 70% of the time.

workedSteps.text: The majority is right if all three are right or exactly two are. Write the chance of each case, using p = 0.7 and 1 − p = 0.3.
Exactly two right: there are three ways to choose the two, and each has probability 0.7 × 0.7 × 0.3.
All three right: 0.7 × 0.7 × 0.7.
The majority is right in either case, so the two chances add.

steps.headline: Find the chance that a majority of three independent voters is right when each is right 60% of the time.

workedSteps.text: Use the same two cases, with p = 0.6 and 1 − p = 0.4.
Exactly two right: there are three ways to choose the two, and each way has probability 0.6 × 0.6 × 0.4.
All three right: 0.6 × 0.6 × 0.6.
The majority is right in either case, so its chance is the sum of the two.

lead.text: The fourth pattern, **orchestrator-workers**, handles the case in which the subtasks cannot be listed in advance. A central model reads the input, decides what subtasks it needs, hands each to a worker and combines the results. In the figure the task is to update a library call across a codebase, and the number of files to edit depends on the codebase: two for the first input and four for the second. The structure of the work is decided at run time, which is the point at which a workflow begins to resemble an agent.

The fifth, the **evaluator-optimiser**, pairs a call that proposes an answer with a call that critiques it, and repeats the pair until the evaluator accepts. It suits a task with clear criteria that a critic can apply, and it is the workflow form of the reflection pattern from the last lesson. Each round adds two calls of latency, so the loop needs a limit on the number of rounds.

reveal.text: The list of subtasks depends on the input, so a fixed set of branches cannot cover it, and a model has to decide the subtasks after reading the request.

lead.text: In an evaluator-optimiser loop the proposer takes 3 seconds per proposal and the evaluator takes 2 seconds per critique. The evaluator accepts only on the third proposal, so the loop runs three rounds, each with one proposal and one critique, and the calls cannot overlap.

reveal.text: Each round adds five seconds, so the third proposal is accepted only after fifteen. This is why the loop needs a limit on the number of rounds and is used where the extra quality is worth the wait.

lead.text: A team runs five voters to improve an answer. All five are the same model with the same prompt and the temperature set to zero, so that the model gives the same output each time, and the team applies the majority rule.

reveal.text: The formula for a majority applies only when the voters make independent mistakes. Five identical outputs make one answer five times, so the vote adds cost and no accuracy.

lessons.orientation: Match a task to a workflow pattern and compute the latency and accuracy effects of parallel branches and votes.
lessons.nextAction: Divide work between several agents, and see what the division costs.

blocks.text: A support system might use several model calls on one request: a call to classify it, calls to draft the parts of a reply, a call to check the tone and a call to merge the parts. How those calls are arranged decides how long the customer waits, how much each reply costs and how accurate the answer is, and there are five standard arrangements.

Each arrangement is a workflow in the sense of the first lesson, because code fixes the structure, though the last two begin to blur the line with an agent. Knowing the arrangements lets you predict the wait, the bill and the accuracy of a design before anything is built.

diagram.alt: Five workflow patterns drawn as small diagrams: prompt chaining, a fixed sequence of calls; routing, in which a classifier picks one specialist; parallelisation, with independent branches and a merge; orchestrator-workers, in which an orchestrator plans subtasks at run time; and evaluator-optimiser, in which a proposer and an evaluator loop until accepted.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to match a task to one of five workflow patterns, work out the time of parallel branches, and compute the accuracy of a majority vote.
intro.whyItMatters: The pattern chosen sets latency, cost and accuracy, and two of its effects are often mis-estimated.

recap.keyIdea: Five patterns compose model calls in code, parallel branches take the time of the slowest, and a vote helps only when independent voters are each better than chance.

blocks.text: Chaining and routing fix the path of model calls, parallel branches finish when the slowest does without costing less, and a majority of three independent 80% voters is right about 90% of the time. An orchestrator decides its subtasks at run time, which a fixed workflow cannot, and an evaluator loop adds two calls of latency to every round. A pattern is worth its cost when the task has the shape that it was designed for, and a vote of identical copies does not.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson divides work among several agents and counts what the division costs in tokens and context.

lessons.title: Multiple agents

lead.text: In the **orchestrator-worker** arrangement that Anthropic describes for its research system, a lead agent plans the task, starts a **subagent** for each search, and synthesises what they return. The workers run at the same time, so the elapsed time follows the slowest search, and each starts with a clean context that contains only its own task.

The figure draws the arrangement with token bars: the lead spends 10 thousand tokens on the plan, each of four workers spends 20 thousand, and the lead spends another 10 thousand on the synthesis. Anthropic reported that a system built this way beat a single strong model by 90.2% on its internal research evaluation.

reveal.text: The workers account for 75 of the 95 thousand tokens, and the lead's two stages for the remaining 20. Removing one worker would cut the run to 70 thousand, but it would also cut the searching by a third.

The summary is thirty times smaller than the material behind it. That is what keeps the lead's context small, and it is also why the lead cannot answer a question about a detail that the summary left out.

lead.text: The split also has a price, and the arithmetic shows the largest part of it. Suppose a single agent could do the same research serially in about 40 thousand tokens, an assumption we make for the comparison. The research run drawn at the start of the lesson used 100 thousand in all, so it spent two and a half times the tokens to save time and to keep each search's pages out of one shared context. Anthropic's account is consistent with this: it reports that agents typically use about four times the tokens of a chat interaction and that multi-agent systems use about fifteen times as many, and it concludes that such systems suit tasks whose value is high enough to pay for that.

Two other costs are less visible. A worker's findings reach the lead as a summary, and a summary drops detail, which the lead cannot recover. And each added agent adds an interface at which messages can be malformed or misunderstood, so the number of ways to fail rises with the number of agents. More agents do not mean more intelligence in the system. They mean more work done at the same time, and the work is worth doing only if the task divides into independent parts, which is why Anthropic notes that tasks in which agents depend closely on one another, such as much coding work, are a poor fit.

reveal.text: The multi-agent run costs about 2.9 times as many tokens. The ratio is reasonable if the answer arrives sooner and is better, and wasteful if a single agent would have done as well.

lead.text: A worker does not share the lead's context. It is created with a brief, which is a short statement of its task, and from then on it holds only that brief and the results of its own searches. This is **context isolation**, and it follows that the lead has to write each brief carefully, since anything it does not say is something the worker cannot know.

Isolation also separates a subagent from a **handoff**, in which one agent passes control of the whole conversation, with its context, to another that then carries on with the user. In a handoff the receiving agent takes over, whereas a subagent returns a result and the lead stays in charge.

diagram.alt: Two views of what each agent holds. The lead agent holds the question, the plan and four short summaries. One worker holds only its brief and its own searches, and does not hold the lead's plan, the other workers' searches or the full question.

reveal.text: A narrow brief keeps the worker on its own task and keeps the lead's context small. It also puts the burden on the lead to say what the worker needs, because nothing else reaches it.

lead.text: Because the agents share nothing except the messages between them, the messages need an agreed form, which is the **agent contract**: the defined inputs, outputs and permissions between two agents. The *input* is the task and whatever the worker needs to do it. The *output schema* is the exact shape of what it returns, such as a list of claims, each with its text and a source address. The *tools allowed* is a list of the tools it may call, and the *budget* is its limit on tokens and tool calls. Because the lead can check a returned message against the schema, a malformed result is caught at the boundary and not discovered in the synthesis.

The contract settles one further question, which is who owns each piece of state. If two workers edit one notes file at the same time, the later write can overwrite the earlier, so a safer design has each worker return its result to the lead, and has the lead, as the only writer, merge the results into the shared record.

steps.headline: Check a worker's reply against its contract, and count the claims that meet it.

workedSteps.text: The contract says every claim must have a text and a `source_url`. The worker returns three claims: A has both, B has a text and no source, and C has both.
Test each claim against the schema. Claim A passes, and claim B fails because it has no `source_url`.
Claim C has both fields, so it passes.
Two of the three claims meet the contract.

reveal.text: Several agents pay off when the work can run in parallel or the material is too large for one context. A single agent can read a 20-page document, so the extra agents would only add tokens.

lead.text: Three research workers are told to record the sources they find in one shared list, and all three work at the same moment. Each reads the list, adds its own sources, and saves the whole list back.

reveal.text: One save overwrites another, so some sources are lost without any error being reported. The remedy is an owner: workers return their sources to the lead, and one agent writes the list.

lessons.orientation: Say when splitting work between agents helps, count the token cost, and define the contract between agents.
lessons.nextAction: Give an agent the right permissions, and make its riskiest actions governed.

blocks.text: A research question needs four independent searches. One agent could run them one after another, with every page it reads piling up in its context, or a lead agent could hand one search to each of four workers that run at the same time. In Anthropic's account of its research system the second arrangement beat a single agent by a wide margin on its own tests, and it also used many more tokens, so whether it was a good bargain depended on what the extra tokens bought.

Splitting the work buys time and keeps each search's pages out of a single crowded context, and it is paid for in tokens, in the detail that a worker's summary leaves out, and in every message between agents that can be misread. Counting those costs is how you decide whether a second agent is worth adding, and it also shows what the lead has to tell each worker for the split to work at all.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say when splitting work between agents helps, count the tokens a multi-agent run uses, and write the contract between a lead and its workers.
intro.whyItMatters: Multi-agent designs trade tokens for speed and focus, so their cost has to be counted and the boundary between agents has to be defined.

recap.keyIdea: Splitting work among agents buys parallel time and clean contexts, costs tokens and an interface that can fail, and works only if each worker's brief and contract say exactly what is passed.

blocks.text: A lead agent can split a task among workers that run at the same time, each with its own context, at the price of the tokens every worker uses and of the detail that summaries drop. A worker sees only what it is handed, so the lead's brief decides what it can do, and the contract fixes the input, the output schema, the tools allowed and the budget. Shared state needs a single owner, since agents that write to one record at once can overwrite each other.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns from how agents are built to how they are governed, starting with the permissions an agent holds.

lessons.title: Permissions and governed actions

lead.text: A support agent has tools that range from harmless to serious: it can search orders, read the policy, issue refunds, send emails and delete accounts. The first design step is to sort them into **tiers** by what a wrong call would cost. A read tool is the first tier, a small write that can be tolerated or undone, such as a refund of $20 or less, is the second tier, and a costly or permanent write, such as a larger refund, an email that cannot be unsent or a deletion, is the third.

In the figure reads need no approval, a refund of up to $20 runs and is logged, a refund over $20 and an email need a person to approve them before they run, and deleting an account is never offered to the agent at all. The structure is what OWASP's guidance on *excessive agency* asks for: limit the tools an agent is given, limit what each can do, and require a person's approval for actions of high impact.

diagram.alt: A table of six tool rows for a support agent with a tier and an approval rule for each. The two read tools need no approval. A refund of up to 20 dollars runs and is logged. A refund over 20 dollars and sending an email need a person to approve. Deleting an account is never offered to the agent.

agent</text></svg>

reveal.text: A payment of this size cannot easily be taken back, and the cost of a wrong call falls on the company, so a person has to decide it. The other three are reads or drafts that can be corrected.

lead.text: It is tempting to state the rules in the system prompt, for instance by telling the agent never to refund more than $20. A prompt is only text that the model reads, and the model may not follow it: an unexpected input, a long conversation or an injected instruction can lead it to ignore the rule. A permission that the model can choose to break is a request, and not a control.

The check therefore belongs in the code that runs the tool, as the figure shows. The model sends its call, and a policy check on the server compares the call with the rule for its tier before anything runs. A $15 refund passes and is recorded. A $150 refund stops at the check, is recorded as blocked and waits for a person's decision, and the tool never runs. OWASP's guidance describes the same principle as complete mediation, which means that requests are authorised in the downstream system and not left to the model to decide. The agent should also have its *own* identity, with only the access its task needs, rather than borrowing the signed-in user's full credentials, so that a mistake or an attack reaches only as far as that identity does. This is **least privilege**.
