reveal.text: Listing who the agent serves and what could go wrong comes first, because measuring and managing both need a list of risks to act on.

steps.headline: Work out how many actions a person reviews in a day when the three tiers of actions get different oversight.

workedSteps.text: The agent makes 1,500 actions a day: 1,200 reads, 250 small writes and 50 costly writes. Reads are sampled at 1%, small writes at 4%, and every costly write is approved first.
Reads: 1% of 1,200 is 12 actions to read. Small writes: 4% of 250 is 10 actions to read.
Costly writes: every one of the 50 is approved before it runs, so a person sees all 50.
A person looks at the sampled reads, the sampled small writes and every costly write.

steps.headline: Work out the daily reviews for 1,000 actions a day: 800 reads sampled at 2%, 180 small writes sampled at 5%, and 20 costly writes all approved.

workedSteps.text: Reads: 2% of 800 is 16 actions.
Small writes: 5% of the 180 small writes are sampled for a person to read.
Costly writes: all 20 are approved first.
A person looks at the sampled reads, the sampled small writes and every costly write.

lead.text: A team decides that a person must approve each of the 2,400 actions its agent makes in a day, because a human in the loop is always safer. The approvers are three staff members who each handle about 800 approvals a day, one every few seconds.

reveal.text: At that speed the approval is a reflex, so it adds delay without adding a check. The sturdier design approves the few risky actions, samples the rest, and watches for anomalies, which puts attention where it can be used.

lessons.orientation: Place human control points, stage a rollout, and map an agent's risk work onto the NIST AI RMF functions.
lessons.nextAction: Choose a level of autonomy for an agent, back it with evidence, and write down the triggers that would change it.

blocks.text: An agent that makes 1,500 actions a day cannot have every action read by a person, and a design that pretends otherwise gives a person a few seconds per action and a habit of approving without looking. The question is where a person's limited attention does the most good, and when the agent has earned the right to act without being asked.

The autonomy ladder gives the answer a shape, since an agent can be moved up it one rung at a time, from proposing actions that nobody carries out to acting alone within its permissions. What makes each move safe is evidence gathered on the rung below, such as how often the agent's proposals matched what people decided, together with a condition, written down in advance, under which the agent steps back down.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to place oversight points, set the gates of a staged rollout, and match risk tasks to the functions of the NIST framework.
intro.whyItMatters: An agent's autonomy should be raised on evidence and lowered on triggers decided in advance, and the oversight that supports it has to be sized for the people who do it.

recap.keyIdea: Oversight is placed where a person's attention helps most, autonomy is raised by stages gated on evidence, and a written record states the level and the triggers that change it.

blocks.text: A person can approve before an action, review a sample after it, or be alerted and stop the agent, and sampling a few percent of a large volume keeps the review within a person's attention. A rollout moves from shadow to assist to act on evidence such as 95% agreement with human decisions, and it moves back when a sampled error rate crosses its limit. The decision record states the level and both triggers, and the NIST functions of Govern, Map, Measure and Manage show who owns which part of the risk work.

questions.prompt: A refund workflow makes 3 model calls per request at $0.01 a call. An agent built for the same task averages 12 calls at the same price, because every tool result is followed by another model call. Roughly how does the agent's cost per request compare with the workflow's?
hints: Both designs pay the same price per call, so compare the numbers of calls.
questions.onCorrect: Both designs pay the same price per call, so the cost ratio is simply the ratio of the numbers of calls, 12 to 3.

acceptedIdeas: About four times as much
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About four times as much

choices.label: About four times as much
A little more, since only the agent's extra tool calls are charged
About twelve times as much
About the same, since both use the same model at the same price

misconceptions.feedback: The price per call is the same, but the agent makes 12 calls where the workflow makes 3, and the number of calls is what sets the cost.
Every one of the agent's 12 model calls is charged at $0.01, against 3 for the workflow, so the extra calls are most of the bill and not a small addition to it.
Twelve is the agent's number of calls, but the workflow makes 3 of its own, so the agent costs 12 to 3, or four times as much.

questions.prompt: What does the workflow cost for 1,000 requests, in dollars?
hints: Use the cost of one request from the line above.
Scaling a cost to a month means multiplying by the number of requests.
questions.onCorrect: The month's cost is the per-request cost scaled by volume, which is why a small difference per request matters at high volume.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each request costs $0.03, and 1,000 × $0.03 = $30.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the cost of one request. Multiply it by the 1,000 requests.
Check the multiplication: 1,000 × $0.03 has one fewer zero than that.

questions.prompt: What should the team do?
hints: Ask which rung is the lowest one that meets this need.
Count what each higher rung would add: calls, waiting time, a person.
questions.onCorrect: A fixed lookup and a template need no model decisions, so the lowest rung that meets the need is code with a fixed path.

acceptedIdeas: Build it in code with a fixed path, since the steps never vary
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Build it in code with a fixed path, since the steps never vary

choices.label: Build an agent, because an agent can also handle the simple case
Build a copilot, so that a person approves each answer
Build it in code with a fixed path, since the steps never vary

misconceptions.feedback: An agent could do it, but it pays for flexibility the task never uses, in extra calls, waiting time and a path that is harder to audit.
A copilot puts a person on every answer, which costs time on a task where the code already knows what to do.

questions.prompt: What does the day cost in dollars?
hints: Find how many of the 2,000 requests go to the agent, then how many take the workflow.
120 requests go to the agent and 1,880 take the workflow.
Price each group at its own cost per request and add the two.
questions.onCorrect: The mixed design costs $70.80 a day, against $60 if every request took the workflow and $240 if every request went to the agent.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 6% of 2,000 is 120 requests at $0.12, which is $14.40. The other 1,880 requests at $0.03 cost $56.40, and $14.40 + $56.40 = $70.80.

misconceptions.feedback: That prices all 2,000 requests at the workflow's $0.03. The agent's 120 requests cost more.
That sends every request to the agent. Only 6% go there.
That is the agent's share only. Add the workflow's 1,880 requests.

questions.prompt: A company is deciding, for six jobs, whether a fixed workflow is enough or whether the model has to choose the steps. Which design suits each job?
hints: Ask, for each job, whether you could write its steps down before the input arrives.
If what one step finds decides the next step, code cannot hold the path.
questions.onCorrect: A job whose steps can be listed in advance belongs in code, with the model called inside it. Only a job whose next step depends on what the last one found needs a model that chooses.

items.label: Each invoice is matched to its purchase order, checked against the same three rules and filed
items.explanation: The steps and their order are known before any invoice arrives, so code can hold them.

items.label: A developer asks any question about a large codebase, and the system searches, reads files and runs tests until it can answer
items.explanation: What to read next depends on what the last file showed, so the model has to choose.

items.label: Each support email is put into one of four categories and the matching template is filled in
items.explanation: Classifying and filling a template are the same steps for every email.

items.label: A research request where the sources to read cannot be known until the first ones have been read
items.explanation: The next search comes from what was just found, which cannot be written in advance.

items.label: Every night, yesterday's tickets are summarised in the same five steps
items.explanation: A fixed nightly sequence is the plainest case for code that calls the model inside it.

items.label: A failing build is fixed by trying a change, running the tests and choosing the next change from the output
items.explanation: Each change depends on the test output, so the path is decided during the run.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The workflow jobs are the invoice matching, the email categories and the nightly summary. The agent jobs are the codebase question, the research request and the failing build.

questions.prompt: A team replaces its five-step expense report process with an agent so that it can handle anything. The five steps never change. After a month each report costs four times as much, and a few reports skip the tax check. What does this show?
hints: Ask who decides the order of the steps in the old process and who decides it now.
What did the extra freedom buy for a task whose steps never change?
questions.onCorrect: When the steps never vary, a workflow gives the same result at a fraction of the cost. The agent paid for a freedom the task did not use.

acceptedIdeas: The task never needed the model to choose its steps, so the agent added cost and error
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The task never needed the model to choose its steps, so the agent added cost and error

choices.label: The agent needs a bigger context window so that it can remember the five steps
The task never needed the model to choose its steps, so the agent added cost and error
The agent needs more tools so that it can find the tax check on its own, without a person
The skipped checks show that agents cannot be trusted with any finance work at all

misconceptions.feedback: The steps are fixed and known, so remembering them is not the problem. Code would run the tax check on every report and could not skip it.
The agent skips the check because it decides whether to run it. A fixed path in code removes that decision.
This is one task whose steps never vary. It says nothing about work where the path depends on what is found; the fault is the rung chosen for this task.

questions.prompt: A coding tool shows the change the model proposes and applies it only after the developer clicks accept. Which rung of the autonomy ladder is this?
hints: Ask who decides whether the proposed change is applied.
One rung has the model propose and a person approve, edit or reject.
questions.onCorrect: A copilot keeps a person between the proposal and the action, which is what separates it from an agent.

acceptedIdeas: copilot
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: copilot

misconceptions.feedback: In an agent no person sits between the model's choice and the action. Here the developer's click is that check.
In a workflow code fixes the order of the steps. Here the model proposes the change and a person decides whether it goes ahead.

questions.prompt: A run is logged as five steps. Steps 1 to 4 are each a tool call: `search_orders`, `read_policy`, `issue_refund` and `send_email`. Step 5 is a plain-text reply with no tool call. The provider bills each model call. How many model calls does the run contain?
hints: Every pass of the loop starts by sending the context to the model.
The code runs the tool calls. Ask what runs on the pass that ends with the reply.
questions.onCorrect: The loop makes one model call per pass and the last pass writes the answer, so five passes are five billed calls and four tool runs.

acceptedIdeas: Five, one at every step including the one that wrote the reply
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Five, one at every step including the one that wrote the reply

choices.label: Four, one for each tool call, since the reply is not a call of its own
Nine, one for each step and one for each tool result
Five, one at every step including the one that wrote the reply

misconceptions.feedback: The reply is the model's output on the fifth pass, so a fifth call produced it, with the context from the first four.
A tool result is added to the context and read by the next call. It does not trigger a call of its own.

questions.prompt: An agent's log shows step 1 calling `get_order(id="A-77")` and getting `error: timeout`. Steps 2 to 9 make the identical call and get the identical error. Nothing in the code limits the run. Which change ends a loop like this whatever the model decides?
hints: Ask which fix still works if the model never decides it is finished.
Look for the option that sets a limit in code instead of changing what the model is likely to write.
questions.onCorrect: A step budget stops the run whatever the model does, which is why Anthropic's guidance on agents recommends stopping conditions such as a maximum number of iterations.

acceptedIdeas: Set a step budget in the code that ends the run after a fixed number of calls
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Set a step budget in the code that ends the run after a fixed number of calls

choices.label: Raise the temperature so that the model is less likely to repeat itself
Add a line to the prompt telling the model to stop whenever a tool keeps failing
Give the agent a second tool that does the same job as `get_order`
Set a step budget in the code that ends the run after a fixed number of calls

misconceptions.feedback: A higher temperature changes how likely a repeat is and cannot rule one out. The limit has to be code that holds whatever the model writes.
A prompt line asks the model to stop, and a model that is stuck may not comply. A limit in code ends the run either way.
A second tool gives the loop one more thing to call. The run goes on for as long as the model keeps choosing.

questions.prompt: A team budgets a ten-step run as ten times the cost of one step, which reads 1,000 tokens. In fact the context grows by 400 tokens at every step. How does the run's input compare with the team's assumption?
hints: The model keeps nothing between calls, so each call reads the whole context again.
List what steps 1, 2 and 10 read, then ask whether ten steps can cost ten times the first.
questions.onCorrect: The ten inputs run from 1,000 to 4,600 tokens and add to 28,000, so long runs cost far more than a flat estimate suggests.

acceptedIdeas: It is 2.8 times larger, about 28,000 tokens against 10,000
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is 2.8 times larger, about 28,000 tokens against 10,000

choices.label: It is the same, since the provider charges the same for each call
It is about 1.4 times larger, because the context grows by 400 tokens, 40% more
It is 2.8 times larger, about 28,000 tokens against 10,000

misconceptions.feedback: The charge follows the tokens read, and each call reads the whole context again, so later calls cost more than the first.
The growth is added at every step and not once. The tenth step alone reads 4,600 tokens.

questions.prompt: Each step of an agent's run succeeds 90% of the time, independently of the others, and a step that fails spoils the run. Roughly how often does a run of three steps succeed?
hints: A run succeeds only if the first, the second and the third steps all succeed.
questions.onCorrect: Independent chances that must all hold multiply, so reliability falls with every step added.

acceptedIdeas: About 75%, a little lower than for one step
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 75%, a little lower than for one step

choices.label: About 90%, the same as for one step, since the steps do not interact
About 75%, a little lower than for one step
About 30%, close to one run in three, since each step loses 10 points

misconceptions.feedback: The run needs all three steps to succeed, and each carries its own 10% chance of failing, so the run fails more often than any single step does.
Each step fails only one time in ten, so most runs still get through all three steps. The chance of finishing falls, but not that far.

questions.prompt: What is 0.98 to the power 20, to two decimal places?
hints: Raise 0.98 to the power 20 on a calculator.
The result is below 0.7.
Round the result to two decimal places.
questions.onCorrect: A step that fails only 2% of the time still leaves a 20-step run failing about one time in three.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 0.98²⁰ is about 0.6676, which is 0.67 to two decimal places.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chance for a single step. The calculation is for 20 steps.
That is the chance that the run fails. The question asks for the chance that it succeeds.

questions.prompt: About how often do all ten steps succeed now?
hints: The run succeeds only if every one of the ten steps succeeds.
Chances of independent events multiply, so start from 0.99 and raise it to a power.
questions.onCorrect: Ten steps at 99% finish about 90% of the time, against about 60% at 95%, so a small gain per step becomes a large gain over the run.

acceptedIdeas: About 90%, since ten steps at 99% multiply to 0.99 to the power 10
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 90%, since ten steps at 99% multiply to 0.99 to the power 10

choices.label: About 99%, the same as one step, since every step is 99% reliable
About 80%, losing two points for each extra step in the run
About 90%, since ten steps at 99% multiply to 0.99 to the power 10

misconceptions.feedback: The steps multiply. A run that needs all ten is less likely to finish than any single step is to succeed.
The loss is not a fixed number of points per step. The chances multiply, and 0.99 ten times over leaves about 90%.

questions.prompt: What is the largest total number of input tokens the model can read over the 8 steps?
hints: The input to step 8 is 1,000 plus seven increases of 400.
Add the eight inputs together.
questions.onCorrect: Capping the steps caps the input: a budget turns the cost of a run from an open question into a number that can be set in advance.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The inputs run from 1,000 to 3,800 in steps of 400, and their sum is 8 × 1,000 + 400 × (0 + 1 + … + 7) = 8,000 + 11,200 = 19,200.

misconceptions.feedback: That keeps the context at 1,000 tokens for all eight steps. It grows by 400 each step.
That is the input to the last step only. Every step's input is billed.
That is the total for three steps. The budget here is eight.

questions.prompt: A team measures each step of its agent at 97% and plans runs of 30 steps. The steps are independent, so about four runs in ten finish. Which change raises the share of runs that finish most?
hints: Thirty chances at 97% multiply to about 40%. Ask what would remove a chance to fail.
Which option lets the code catch a bad step before the run carries on?
questions.onCorrect: A check after a risky step turns a failure into a repair, so the run no longer needs every step to succeed first time.

acceptedIdeas: Check the result after the riskiest steps and redo a step that failed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Check the result after the riskiest steps and redo a step that failed

choices.label: Add a line to the system prompt asking the model to take extra care at every step
Raise the step budget from 30 to 60 so the agent has more room
Check the result after the riskiest steps and redo a step that failed
Let the agent carry on after a failed step and judge only the final answer

misconceptions.feedback: The 97% already includes whatever care the model takes. A longer prompt gives the code no way to notice or repair a failed step.
More steps mean more chances to fail, so the share that finish falls further.
A failed step still spoils the answer. Catching it early is what stops the chances from multiplying.

questions.prompt: In what order do the parts of one pass through an agent loop happen?
hints: The model never runs the tool. Who does?
The result has to be in the context before the next call, because the model keeps nothing between calls.
questions.onCorrect: The model only chooses; the code runs the tool and grows the context. That longer context is why each pass costs more than the one before.

items: The code sends the goal and everything so far to the model
The model replies with a call to one of its tools
The code runs the tool and collects its result
The code adds the call and the result to the context
The model is called again with the longer context

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The code sends the context, the model replies with a tool call, the code runs it and adds the call and result to the context, and the model is called again with the longer context.

questions.prompt: The code around an agent ends every run after 25 model calls, whatever the model says. What is this limit called?
hints: It is enforced by the code, not by the model.
Its name says what it limits and what kind of allowance it is.
questions.onCorrect: A step budget holds even when the model never decides it is finished.

acceptedIdeas: step budget
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: step budget

misconceptions.feedback: Temperature changes how the model samples its words. It does not limit the run.
The window is the most the model can read at once. The limit here counts calls and is set by the code.

questions.prompt: A support team adds a tool, `cancel_subscription(customer_id)`, which ends a customer's plan from the next billing date. Which kind of tool is it?
hints: Ask whether the shop is the same after the call as before it.
A tool that ends a plan changes a record, even if the change takes effect later.
questions.onCorrect: A tool that changes a record outside the conversation is a write tool, and that is true of any tool that cancels, creates, sends or pays.

acceptedIdeas: A write tool, because it changes the customer's plan
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A write tool, because it changes the customer's plan

misconceptions.feedback: A tool can change things without moving money. Ending a plan changes what the customer is billed.
The plan does end, and a change that takes effect later is still a change. A read tool leaves everything as it was.

choices.label: A read tool, because it does not move any money
A read tool, because nothing changes until the next billing date
A write tool, because it changes the customer's plan

questions.prompt: A write tool, `issue_refund(order_id, amount)`, pays out on every call. The agent calls it, the refund goes through, and the reply is lost in a network timeout. Hearing nothing, the agent calls it twice more, and both retries reach the server. How many refunds does the customer receive?
hints: Ask what the server can see in each call that would tell it the call is a repeat.
questions.onCorrect: A write tool with no memory of earlier calls treats every request as new, so a retry after a lost reply pays again.

acceptedIdeas: Three, one for each call that reached the server
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Three, one for each call that reached the server

choices.label: One, because the server can tell that the later calls are repeats
None, because the agent never received a confirmation
Three, one for each call that reached the server

misconceptions.feedback: Each call carries only an order and an amount, so nothing in it lets the server tell a retry from a new request, and it pays out every time.
The first call succeeded at the server even though its reply was lost, and a lost reply does not undo a payment that has already been made.

questions.prompt: How many refunds did the server make?
hints: A refund is made only when the server sees a key for the first time.
The calls used two different keys.
Count the distinct keys.
questions.onCorrect: The number of refunds equals the number of distinct keys, however many times each is sent.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only the first call with each distinct key makes a refund: keys a and b, so 2.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts every call. Calls that repeat a stored key make no refund.
The calls carry only two distinct keys, a and b.

questions.prompt: What happens to the second refund, the $15?
hints: Check whether the two calls carry the same key or different keys.
The server makes a refund only the first time it sees a key.
questions.onCorrect: A key that is shared by two different actions makes the server treat the second as a retry of the first, and the second action is silently dropped.

acceptedIdeas: The server skips it as a repeat, so the $15 is never paid
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The server skips it as a repeat, so the $15 is never paid

misconceptions.feedback: The server compares the key and nothing else, and both calls carry `refund-4471`.
The key is the only thing the server checks, and the day of the call is not part of it.

choices.label: The server makes it, because the amount differs from the first call
The server makes it, because the call arrives on a different day
The server skips it as a repeat, so the $15 is never paid

questions.prompt: An agent calls `search_orders(date="last Tuesday")` and gets back `400`. It makes the same call three more times and gives up. The tool's description reads "Searches orders." Which change helps most?
hints: The model reads the tool description before the call and the error after it. Which of those could tell it the format?
A model that gets `400` has nothing to change. What would let it change the argument?
questions.onCorrect: A description that states the format, and an error that says what was wrong, let the model correct the call. Anthropic's advice is to write a tool definition like a docstring for a junior developer.

acceptedIdeas: Give the description a date format and return an error that names it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Give the description a date format and return an error that names it

choices.label: Raise the step budget so that the agent can try the call more times
Tell the model in the system prompt to be careful to use dates correctly
Give the description a date format and return an error that names it
Return a bare `Error` so the model cannot be misled by the message

misconceptions.feedback: More attempts of the same call return the same `400`, and nothing in the result tells the model what to change.
A general instruction does not say which format this tool accepts. The description and the error are what the model reads when it calls.
A bare error is the fault here. A model that reads only `400` guesses, and often repeats the call.

questions.prompt: An agent has two tools. `search_orders(query)` is described as "Looks up orders" and `find_orders(text)` as "Finds orders". The agent picks one at random and sometimes sends it the wrong kind of input. What is the best fix?
hints: Two tools with the same job and almost the same description give the model nothing to choose by.
Which fix removes the overlap, or tells the model how the two differ?
questions.onCorrect: A model can only choose between tools that its descriptions set apart. Overlapping tools with vague descriptions turn each call into a guess.

acceptedIdeas: Merge them, or say in each description what it takes and when to use it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Merge them, or say in each description what it takes and when to use it

choices.label: Rename the tools so the names look more different and leave the descriptions alone
Add a third tool that calls both and returns whichever result is better
Merge them, or say in each description what it takes and when to use it
Tell the model in the prompt to always pick the first tool

misconceptions.feedback: The model chooses by reading descriptions. Different names over the same vague descriptions leave the same guess.
A third overlapping tool is one more choice to get wrong, and nothing tells the model which result is better.
That hides the choice and keeps the confusion. When the first tool is wrong for the input, the agent has no way to the second.

questions.prompt: A refund call times out, so the agent sends it again with the same token as the first attempt, and the server pays out once. What is that token called?
hints: It identifies one intended action and travels with every attempt.
Its name says that doing the operation twice has the same effect as doing it once.
questions.onCorrect: The server stores the key, so a retry that carries it is treated as the same refund and is not paid again.

acceptedIdeas: idempotency key
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: idempotency key

misconceptions.feedback: An API key says who is calling. The token here says that two calls are the same request.
A session identifies a connection. This token identifies one intended refund, whichever connection carries it.

questions.prompt: Four applications each use six tools, wired one to one. A seventh tool arrives. What does it cost to connect it to all four applications, wired directly and through a shared protocol?
hints: Count the connections the new server needs to each application when nothing is shared.
With a shared format, ask what the applications already have.
questions.onCorrect: Direct wiring costs one integration per application for each new tool. A shared protocol costs the new tool one implementation.

acceptedIdeas: Four integrations directly, and one implementation with a shared protocol
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Four integrations directly, and one implementation with a shared protocol

choices.label: One integration either way, since it is a single new tool
Four integrations directly, and one implementation with a shared protocol
Seven integrations directly, one for each of the tools in use
Four integrations in both cases, since every application must connect

misconceptions.feedback: Wired directly, each application needs its own connection to the new tool, which makes four.
Seven counts the tools. The new tool needs one connection for each application.
With a shared protocol the applications already speak the format, so the new tool needs only its own implementation.

questions.prompt: A client sends `{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 7, "method": "tools/call", "params": {"name": "search_orders", "arguments": {"email": "ana@example.com"}}}`. What is it asking the server to do?
hints: The `method` member says what is asked. Read its value first.
Then read `params`: what do `name` and `arguments` tell the server to run?
questions.onCorrect: The `method` of `tools/call` asks the server to run the named tool with the given arguments, and the `id` of 7 will come back on the reply.

acceptedIdeas: Run the `search_orders` tool with that email address
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Run the `search_orders` tool with that email address

choices.label: List the tools that the server offers
Say which protocol version and capabilities the client supports
Run the `search_orders` tool with that email address
Tell the server that the client is ready for normal requests

misconceptions.feedback: Listing is the `tools/list` method, and its params carry no tool `name` or `arguments`.
That is the `initialize` request, which is sent once at the start of the session.
That is a notification with no `id`, and it names no tool.

questions.prompt: A host starts a tool server as a separate program on the same machine. What is the simplest channel for the two programs to exchange messages?
hints: A program already has a place where it reads input and a place where it writes output.
questions.onCorrect: The host writes to the server's standard input and reads its standard output, which needs no network at all, and this transport is called stdio.

acceptedIdeas: Through the server's standard input and output, which the host already holds
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Through the server's standard input and output, which the host already holds

choices.label: Over the network, through a web address that the server publishes for clients
Through the server's standard input and output, which the host already holds
Through a shared database that both programs check for new rows at intervals

misconceptions.feedback: A web address is how a remote server is reached, and a program the host has started on its own machine can be reached without any network.
A shared database would need a third program and constant checking for new rows, which is more machinery than two programs on one machine need.

questions.prompt: A company has 6 applications and 9 tool servers. Which pair of figures compares wiring every application to every server with using a shared protocol?
hints: Wiring every application to every server counts pairs.
A shared protocol needs one implementation on each side, so count the applications and the servers once.
questions.onCorrect: Direct wiring costs 6 × 9 = 54 and a shared protocol 6 + 9 = 15. Each new server then costs one implementation, where before it cost six.

acceptedIdeas: 54 direct integrations, against 15 implementations of the protocol
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 54 direct integrations, against 15 implementations of the protocol

choices.label: 15 direct integrations, against 54 implementations of the protocol
54 direct integrations, against 15 implementations of the protocol
15 direct integrations, against 9 implementations of the protocol

misconceptions.feedback: The figures are the wrong way round. Direct wiring multiplies, 6 × 9, and the protocol adds, 6 + 9.
Direct wiring needs a link for every pair, 6 × 9. The protocol needs one implementation for each application and each server, 6 + 9.

questions.prompt: Which pairing of protocol and job is right?
hints: Ask which of the two is a tool and which is an agent that decides for itself.
One of these protocols connects agents to tools and data.
questions.onCorrect: A tool server runs what it is told and an agent decides for itself, which is the line between MCP and A2A.

acceptedIdeas: A2A for the hotel booking and MCP for the timetable lookup
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A2A for the hotel booking and MCP for the timetable lookup

choices.label: MCP for the hotel booking and A2A for the timetable lookup
MCP for both, since both involve calling something outside the agent
A2A for the hotel booking and MCP for the timetable lookup
A2A for both, since both systems belong to other companies

misconceptions.feedback: The timetable system is a plain tool, and the hotel chain's agent decides for itself, so the two are the wrong way round.
MCP treats the other side as a tool server, and the hotel chain's agent plans and decides for itself.
The timetable system is a tool and has no goals of its own, which is what MCP serves.

questions.prompt: A user works in a chat application that reaches an order system and an email system through MCP. Which part of MCP is each of these?
hints: Ask which part the user sees, which part carries messages and which part runs code.
A client talks to one server, so look for the part that sends or holds a connection.
questions.onCorrect: The host contains the model, a client holds each connection, and the server holds the tools and runs them.

items.label: The chat application the user types in, which contains the model
items.explanation: The host is the application the user works in, and the model lives in it.

items.label: The connection that holds the link to the order system and speaks the protocol for the host
items.explanation: A client holds one connection to one server on the host's behalf.

items.label: The program that lists `search_orders` and runs it when a call arrives
items.explanation: The server offers the tools and holds their code.

items.label: The window that shows a confirmation before a tool call goes ahead
items.explanation: The specification leaves confirmation to the application, which is the host.

items.label: The program that holds the code of the email tool and returns its result
items.explanation: Running the tool is the server's job, never the model's or the client's.

items.label: The part that sends `tools/call` to the email system for the model
items.explanation: The client carries the call to its server. It does not run the tool.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The host is the chat application and its confirmation window. The clients are the connection and the sender of `tools/call`. The servers are the program that runs `search_orders` and the email tool program.

questions.prompt: A host connects to a new tool server, and the model then uses one of its tools. In what order do the messages go?
hints: The two sides must agree on a version and on capabilities before anything else.
The model can only choose a tool after it has read the descriptions that `tools/list` returns.
questions.onCorrect: The specification requires initialisation first, and a client calls a tool only after the list has told the model what exists.

items: The client sends `initialize` with its protocol version and capabilities
The server answers with its own version and capabilities
The client sends the notification that it is ready
The client sends `tools/list` and receives the tool descriptions
The client sends `tools/call` for the tool the model chose

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The client sends `initialize`, the server answers, the client sends the ready notification, then `tools/list` returns the descriptions, and last `tools/call` runs the chosen tool.

questions.prompt: A tool call reaches the server, and the underlying API refuses it with "rate limit exceeded; try again in 60 seconds". The server replies with a result in which `isError` is `true` and that text. Why does it use a result and not a JSON-RPC error?
hints: Ask who reads a tool result and who reads a protocol error.
The tool did run. Which kind of error is that?
questions.onCorrect: A failure inside a tool is reported in the result so that the model can read it. A request the server cannot understand comes back as a JSON-RPC error.

acceptedIdeas: The model can read the message and decide what to do, such as waiting
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The model can read the message and decide what to do, such as waiting

choices.label: The request was malformed, and a result with `isError` is how that is reported
The model can read the message and decide what to do, such as waiting
The flag makes the client repeat the call after the delay it names

misconceptions.feedback: A malformed request or an unknown tool is a protocol error. Here the request was fine and the tool ran and failed.
The flag only says that the tool ran and failed. The model or the code decides whether to try again.

questions.prompt: An agent has a window of 200,000 tokens and compacts its context when usage reaches 75% of the window. Its context now holds 120,000 tokens. How many more tokens can be added before compaction triggers?
hints: Find the token count at which compaction triggers.
75% of 200,000 tokens is the trigger.
Subtract the tokens already in use from the trigger.
questions.onCorrect: Compaction is triggered by a count of tokens, which is why a single large tool result can set it off at any step.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the room left in the whole window, 200,000 − 120,000. Compaction triggers earlier, at 75% usage.
That is the trigger point. The question asks how much room is left before it.
That is 25% of the window. The trigger is at 75% of it.

questions.prompt: An agent's history of 30,000 tokens is replaced by a summary of 1,500 tokens. What can the summary hold?
hints: Compare the two sizes: the summary has one token for every twenty in the history.
questions.onCorrect: Which details survive depends on what the summariser is told to keep, and that instruction is part of the design.

acceptedIdeas: The gist of what happened, with most exact values left out
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The gist of what happened, with most exact values left out

choices.label: All the facts in the history, packed into fewer words without any loss
Only the latest turn, kept exactly as it was written in the history
The gist of what happened, with most exact values left out

misconceptions.feedback: The summary is twenty times shorter than the history, and no rewording packs that much text into a twentieth of the space, so most of the detail has to go.
A summary is written by the model about the whole history, so it covers the earlier turns as well, though in far less detail.

questions.prompt: An agent's context reaches its trigger, so the code has the model rewrite the oldest forty turns as a short summary and keeps the last few turns word for word. What is this step called?
hints: The agent is set to do it when usage reaches a threshold.
The name comes from making the context more compact.
questions.onCorrect: Compaction frees room by trading old detail for a summary, so it is set to run before the window is full.

acceptedIdeas: compaction
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: compaction

misconceptions.feedback: Writing a summary is part of it. The name for replacing old turns with one, to free room, is different.

questions.prompt: An agent's window is 200,000 tokens and it compacts at 80% of the window. The history is 62,000 tokens when a tool result of 21,000 tokens arrives. What happens when the result is added?
hints: Find the trigger in tokens first: it is a share of the whole window.
Then add the result to the history and compare the two totals.
questions.onCorrect: The total of 83,000 is well below the trigger of 160,000, so compaction waits. The steps it postpones still re-read the larger context, so the bigger window delays the problem.

acceptedIdeas: Nothing yet: the context is 83,000 tokens and the trigger is 160,000
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Nothing yet: the context is 83,000 tokens and the trigger is 160,000

choices.label: Compaction runs, because the result alone is more than 20,000 tokens
Compaction runs, because 83,000 tokens is more than a third of the window
Nothing yet: the context is 83,000 tokens and the trigger is 160,000

misconceptions.feedback: The trigger compares the total in use with a share of the window. The size of one result does not set it off.
A third is not the threshold. Compaction waits until 160,000 tokens, which is 80% of 200,000.

questions.prompt: What is the most likely result on Wednesday?
hints: Think about what the agent can know about the note beyond its text.
Memory has writes, and nothing in the note says that it has changed.
questions.onCorrect: A memory that is written to can hold a wrong or stale fact, and every later run reads it as though it were true.

acceptedIdeas: The agent treats the note as true and may act on it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The agent treats the note as true and may act on it

choices.label: The note is ignored, because old notes are always discarded
The agent treats the note as true and may act on it
The agent asks the model whether the note is current, and the model knows
The note is corrected automatically when the session starts

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing in the store discards a note because of its age, and the agent will read it when it is relevant.
Nothing in the example updates the note, and the store does not know that the refund was refused.
The model has only the note and its context, so it has no way to know that the review changed the outcome.

questions.prompt: An agent with a 128,000-token window has 100,000 tokens in use and compacts at 80% of the window. It calls a tool that returns a whole 60,000-token log file. Which change to the tool keeps the run healthy?
hints: Add the result to the tokens in use and compare it with the window.
The cure has to act before the tokens enter the context.
questions.onCorrect: A result larger than the room left cannot be rescued afterwards. The tool has to return a part of the log, so the agent reads only what it needs.

acceptedIdeas: Return only the matching lines, or one page of the log at a time
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Return only the matching lines, or one page of the log at a time

choices.label: Raise the compaction trigger to 95% so that the log fits
Let the full log in, since compaction will summarise it afterwards
Ask the model in the prompt to skim the log quickly
Return only the matching lines, or one page of the log at a time

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves less room for the model's reply and for later results, and 160,000 tokens is more than the whole window.
The log still enters the context first, and the next call reads all 60,000 tokens before any summary exists.
The model can only skim what is already in its context. The tokens are paid for when the result arrives.

questions.prompt: An agent was given an invoice number early in a long run. After compaction replaced the early turns with a summary, it queried a different invoice. What is the best fix?
hints: A summary keeps the gist. Ask which kind of fact the agent needs word for word.
Where can a fact live so that it survives both compaction and the end of the run?
questions.onCorrect: Exact values belong in external memory, where nothing rewrites them. The summary can then lose the number without the agent losing it.

acceptedIdeas: Write exact identifiers to external memory and read them back when needed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Write exact identifiers to external memory and read them back when needed

choices.label: Compact more often, so that each summary covers fewer turns of the run
Ask for longer summaries, so that nothing in the early turns is left out
Write exact identifiers to external memory and read them back when needed
Enlarge the window so that compaction never has to happen during the run

misconceptions.feedback: A summary drops exact values whatever its length. More frequent compaction gives more chances to lose them.
A longer summary may keep this number and cannot promise to keep every exact value.
A larger window postpones compaction and does not prevent it, and the number would still be gone in the next run.

questions.prompt: An agent saves the user's preferred reply language to a file with one tool and reads it back in a later session with another. What is this storage called?
hints: It lives outside the window and survives the end of a run.
Its name says where it is kept.
questions.onCorrect: External memory takes no room in the window until the agent reads it, and it lasts across runs.

acceptedIdeas: external memory
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: external memory

misconceptions.feedback: The working context is what is in the prompt on this step. It is gone when the run ends.
Compaction rewrites old turns inside the context. A file the agent reads back later lies outside it.

questions.prompt: A plan-then-execute agent writes an eight-step plan and step 5 fails. In what order does the run go?
hints: Nothing can run before the plan exists.
The agent can only replan after it has seen the failure.
questions.onCorrect: The failure costs one wasted action and one more model call for the new plan, so a replan is not free.

items: The agent writes an eight-step plan
Steps 1 to 4 run and succeed
Step 5 fails
The agent writes a new plan for the work that is left
The new plan runs to the end

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The agent writes the plan, steps 1 to 4 succeed, step 5 fails, the agent writes a new plan for the rest, and that plan runs to the end.

questions.prompt: A form-filling task has eight steps that never change. A reason-act loop makes one model call per step. A plan-then-execute agent writes its plan in one model call and then needs the model in only two of the eight steps, since the other six are mechanical. How do the two compare in model calls?
hints: Count the calls each makes: one per step for the loop, and the plan plus two steps for the other.
questions.onCorrect: Writing the plan once replaces the per-step choice, so the number of calls follows the number of steps that need judgement.

acceptedIdeas: The plan-then-execute agent makes far fewer, under half as many
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The plan-then-execute agent makes far fewer, under half as many

choices.label: The plan-then-execute agent makes far fewer, under half as many
About the same, since both carry out all eight steps
The plan-then-execute agent makes more, since writing the plan is an extra call

misconceptions.feedback: Both carry out eight steps, but six of the plan-then-execute agent's steps are mechanical and need no model, while the loop calls the model at every step.
The plan costs one call, but it saves the loop's call at each of the six mechanical steps, so the total is three calls against eight.

questions.prompt: Which pattern fits setting up the new employee's accounts?
hints: The steps are known in advance, and a failure changes only the tail of the plan.
questions.onCorrect: Predictable steps are what make a plan written first worth its cost, and failures are handled by rewriting its tail.

acceptedIdeas: Plan then execute
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Plan then execute

misconceptions.feedback: A reason-act loop decides each step after the last result, whereas the onboarding steps are known in advance.
Reflection critiques a finished attempt, and the onboarding has no attempt to critique yet.

choices.label: The reason-act loop
Plan then execute
Reflection

questions.prompt: A team wants to find out why a customer's card payments keep being declined. What to check next depends on what each payment record shows, and an early result may change the whole line of enquiry. Which pattern fits best?
hints: Ask whether the steps can be written before the first record is read.
Choose the pattern that decides each step after seeing the last result.
questions.onCorrect: When every observation can change what to do next, a plan written first would be out of date after one step.

acceptedIdeas: The reason-act loop, which picks each next step
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The reason-act loop, which picks each next step

misconceptions.feedback: Reflection critiques a result that already exists, and this task has no result yet.
A plan written first would be out of date as soon as the first payment record is read.

choices.label: The reason-act loop, which picks each next step
Reflection, with a critique after each attempt
Plan then execute, with the steps written first

questions.prompt: How many model calls does the agent make in total?
hints: Count the calls for the first plan and its steps, then the calls for the new plan and its steps.
Each plan costs 1 call, and then 2 steps use the model.
Add the two groups of calls.
questions.onCorrect: Each replan costs a plan call and further model steps, so frequent failures erode the saving that planning first provides.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first plan is 1 call and 2 steps use the model, which is 3. The new plan is 1 call and 2 more steps, which is 3, and 3 + 3 = 6.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count for one plan and its steps. The agent also wrote a second plan.
That counts two plan calls and two model steps, but the new plan again uses the model in two steps.

questions.prompt: What can the reviewer conclude about whether the proposal is right?
hints: The reasoning lines are written by the model, in the same way as its answer.
Ask what outside fact would show that the files are safe to delete.
questions.onCorrect: A reasoning line helps a reader follow a run, but it is not a verified account of how the model reached the action.

acceptedIdeas: Nothing yet, because the reasoning is text and needs a check from outside the model
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Nothing yet, because the reasoning is text and needs a check from outside the model

choices.label: That it is right, because every line of the reasoning looks sound on its own
That it is right, because a longer chain of reasoning is more reliable than a short one
Nothing yet, because the reasoning is text and needs a check from outside the model
That it is wrong, because reasoning shown to a reader is usually a cover for a guess

misconceptions.feedback: The lines look sound, but they are text the model produced, and fluent text can accompany a wrong step.
Length does not make reasoning more reliable. Only a check against an outside fact does that.
The lines are not shown to be a cover for a guess. They simply are not verified evidence.

questions.prompt: A reason-act agent investigates a failed nightly export. Step 1: it reads the job log, which says `disk quota exceeded writing /data/out/part-07`. Step 2: it reasons that old exports probably take the space and calls `delete_files(path="/data/out/*")`, which removes 412 files. Where did the run go wrong?
hints: For each step, ask what the agent had observed before it acted.
A reasoning line is text written by the model. What fact would show that the files could go?
questions.onCorrect: The reasoning at step 2 was plausible, but no observation backed it. A listing of the files' ages, read before the deletion, would have.

acceptedIdeas: At step 2: it acted on a guess, with nothing showing that those files were old exports
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: At step 2: it acted on a guess, with nothing showing that those files were old exports

choices.label: At step 1: it should have planned all the steps in advance, before reading the log
At step 1: it should not have read the log, because job logs can be out of date
At step 2: it acted on a guess, with nothing showing that those files were old exports
Nowhere: the log said the disk was full, and deleting files is how space is freed

misconceptions.feedback: Reading the log first was right, since the next step depended on what it said. A plan written beforehand would have guessed at the cause.
The log was the one observation the agent had. Acting without reading it would have been a guess from the start.
The log showed a quota problem. It did not show which files were safe to delete, and a deletion needs a check from outside the model.

questions.prompt: After a test run fails, an agent writes "my loop stops one item early", changes the code and runs the tests again with that note in its context. Which pattern is this?
hints: The agent acts on a result that already exists.
Its signal comes from outside the model, here the test run.
questions.onCorrect: Reflection turns a failed result into a short critique and tries again with it in context, and it works best when a test supplies the signal.

acceptedIdeas: reflection
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: reflection

misconceptions.feedback: The reason-act loop picks each next step from the last observation. Here the agent critiques a finished attempt and tries it again.
Plan-then-execute writes the steps before acting. This agent had an attempt already and wrote a critique of it.

questions.prompt: A team has six jobs for agents. Which pattern fits each?
hints: Ask whether the steps are known before the first action.
If an outside check tells the agent what was wrong with a finished attempt, think of the pattern that uses it.
questions.onCorrect: The loop fits unknown steps, planning fits known ones, and reflection fits work that an outside check can mark.

items.label: Find which of thirty services is slowing checkout, where each measurement decides the next
items.explanation: The next step depends on what the last measurement showed.

items.label: Onboard a new hire: create the email account, add the groups, order the laptop, the same each time
items.explanation: The steps are known in advance, so a plan can be written once.

items.label: Fix a failing unit test, using the test output to see what went wrong
items.explanation: A test result is an outside signal that a critique can aim at.

items.label: Work out why one customer's invoice total differs from the order, one lookup at a time
items.explanation: Each lookup decides which one comes next.

items.label: Close the month's books in nine fixed steps
items.explanation: A fixed sequence is cheapest to plan once and run.

items.label: Rewrite a function until the linter reports no errors
items.explanation: The linter gives a signal for each attempt, which the next attempt can use.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The loop fits the slow checkout and the invoice difference. Plan then execute fits the onboarding and the month-end close. Reflection fits the failing test and the linter.

questions.prompt: One model call extracts the key facts from a contract, a second turns those facts into a plain-language summary, and a third checks the summary against a list of required points, always in that order. Which pattern is this?
hints: The order of the calls is fixed in code.
The name says what is linked.
questions.onCorrect: In a chain the output of each call becomes the input of the next, so the whole sequence is as predictable as its links.

acceptedIdeas: prompt chaining
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: prompt chaining

misconceptions.feedback: Routing sends the input to one of several specialists. In this task every call runs, in the same order.
An orchestrator chooses subtasks after reading the input, but here the sequence is fixed.

questions.prompt: Three independent branches of a task each need one model call, taking 4 seconds, 6 seconds and 5 seconds. If all three start at the same moment, roughly how long does the task take?
hints: Ask which branch is still running when the other two have finished.
questions.onCorrect: Parallel branches overlap, so the elapsed time is set by the slowest branch rather than by the sum.

acceptedIdeas: About as long as the slowest branch
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About as long as the slowest branch

choices.label: About as long as the three times added together
About as long as the slowest branch
About as long as the quickest branch

misconceptions.feedback: Adding the times is right when the branches run one after another, but these run at the same time, so their times overlap.
The task is not finished until every branch is, so the quickest branch has to wait for the other two.

questions.prompt: A document is checked in three independent sections that start at the same moment and take 7, 3 and 9 seconds. A merge step, which cannot begin until all three have finished, then takes 2 seconds. How long does the whole task take?
hints: Branches that start together finish when the slowest one does.
The merge waits for all of them. What does it add to that time?
questions.onCorrect: The merge stays on the critical path, so the task takes the slowest branch plus the merge.

acceptedIdeas: 11 seconds: the slowest branch, 9, plus the merge, 2
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 11 seconds: the slowest branch, 9, plus the merge, 2

choices.label: 21 seconds, all four steps added together
9 seconds, the slowest branch, since the merge is quick
11 seconds: the slowest branch, 9, plus the merge, 2

misconceptions.feedback: The branches overlap in time, so their durations are not added.
The merge cannot start until the slowest branch ends, so its 2 seconds come after the 9.

questions.prompt: What is the chance that the majority is right? Give it as a decimal.
hints: Add the probability of exactly two right to the probability of all three right.
The two cases are 0.441 and 0.343.
Add the two probabilities, 0.441 and 0.343, to get the chance that the majority is right.
questions.onCorrect: A 70% voter becomes a 78.4% majority, a gain of 8.4 points, against 9.6 points for the 80% voter.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one voter's chance. The question asks for the majority of three.
That is only the exactly-two case. Add the chance that all three are right.

questions.prompt: A user asks for a market report on a product they name, and which sources to search and how many comparisons to make can only be decided once the request has been read. Which pattern serves this best?
hints: Ask which pattern lets the subtasks be decided at run time.
A fixed set of branches or steps is written before the input arrives.
questions.onCorrect: An orchestrator decides the subtasks at run time, which a fixed workflow cannot, since its structure is written in advance.

acceptedIdeas: Orchestrator-workers, where a central model sets the subtasks
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Orchestrator-workers, where a central model sets the subtasks

choices.label: Sectioning, where fixed independent parts run in parallel
Prompt chaining, where each call feeds the next in a fixed order
Routing, where an input is sent to one specialist prompt
Orchestrator-workers, where a central model sets the subtasks

misconceptions.feedback: A chain has a fixed sequence of calls, so it cannot grow or shrink with the input.
Routing picks one of several fixed specialists, and it does not create subtasks.
Sectioning splits a task into parts that the programmer chose before the input arrived.

questions.prompt: How long does the whole loop take?
hints: Work out how long one round takes, a proposal and a critique.
Count the rounds before the evaluator accepts.
questions.onCorrect: Each round adds five seconds and the third proposal is accepted after fifteen, which is why the loop needs a cap on rounds.

acceptedIdeas: 15 seconds: three rounds of 3 + 2, one after another
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 15 seconds: three rounds of 3 + 2, one after another

choices.label: 9 seconds, three rounds of the longer call, since the two calls overlap
15 seconds: three rounds of 3 + 2, one after another
5 seconds, one round, since the evaluator's verdict ends the loop

misconceptions.feedback: The calls cannot overlap. The evaluator needs the proposal first and the proposer needs the critique.
The evaluator accepts only the third proposal, so two earlier rounds of proposal and critique come first.

questions.prompt: What does the vote achieve?
hints: Ask whether the five outputs can differ.
The formula for a majority assumes independent mistakes.
questions.onCorrect: A vote helps only when the voters' errors are independent, and identical copies of one answer repeat the same error.

acceptedIdeas: Nothing, because five identical outputs are one answer repeated
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Nothing, because five identical outputs are one answer repeated

choices.label: It makes the answer faster, because the voters run in parallel
Nothing, because five identical outputs are one answer repeated
It raises the accuracy, as it would for five independent voters
It lowers the accuracy, because more voters means more mistakes

misconceptions.feedback: Parallel voters take the time of the slowest, but they also cost five calls, and the vote still adds no accuracy here.
The formula assumes independent mistakes, and five identical outputs are not independent.
Adding voters does not make each one less accurate. Identical outputs simply add nothing.

questions.prompt: A team has six jobs for workflows. Which pattern from Anthropic's guide fits each?
hints: Ask whether the work is a fixed sequence, a choice between paths, independent parts or a list that depends on the input.
If the subtasks cannot be listed until the input is read, one pattern has a central model decide them.
questions.onCorrect: The patterns differ in who decides the path and when: a chain and a router decide it in code, parallel branches run side by side, and an orchestrator decides after reading the input.

items.label: Draft a product description, translate it, then check the translation against a glossary
items.explanation: Each call reads what the one before produced, in a fixed order.

items.label: Send each message to a billing, technical or sales prompt according to what it asks
items.explanation: An input is classified and sent to one specialised follow-up.

items.label: Check one contract for three unrelated risks at the same time and combine the findings
items.explanation: The three checks do not depend on each other, so they can run together.

items.label: Change a deprecated call in however many files turn out to use it
items.explanation: The list of subtasks is known only after the input has been read.

items.label: Turn a transcript into notes, then turn the notes into an email
items.explanation: A fixed sequence in which each output feeds the next call.

items.label: Answer easy questions with a cheap model and hard ones with a stronger one, after classifying difficulty
items.explanation: A classification decides which path the question takes.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Chaining fits the description with translation and the transcript to email. Routing fits the three-way message split and the easy or hard split. Parallel branches fit the three risk checks. Orchestrator-workers fits the deprecated call.

questions.prompt: In an evaluator-optimiser loop the evaluator keeps finding something new to criticise, and after twelve rounds the draft is no better than it was after three. Which change fits best?
hints: Ask what ends the loop if the evaluator never accepts.
Which option sets a limit in code and keeps the best result?
questions.onCorrect: A cap on rounds bounds the time and the bill, and the loop still returns the best draft it has.

acceptedIdeas: Cap the rounds, and accept the best draft so far at the cap
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Cap the rounds, and accept the best draft so far at the cap

choices.label: Add a second evaluator so that two critics must agree
Cap the rounds, and accept the best draft so far at the cap
Remove the evaluator and send the first draft
Let the loop run until the evaluator accepts, since it will in the end

misconceptions.feedback: Two critics can each find something new, so the loop still has no end and costs twice as much per round.
The first draft is what the loop exists to improve. The fault is the missing limit, not the critique.
Nothing makes the evaluator accept. A limit in code is what ends the loop.

questions.prompt: One call writes a draft, a second call lists its faults, the first rewrites the draft, and this repeats until the second call accepts. Which pattern is this?
hints: One call produces and another judges.
The pattern is named after the two roles.
questions.onCorrect: The loop trades time and tokens for quality, and it needs a cap on rounds.

acceptedIdeas: evaluator-optimiser
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: evaluator-optimiser

misconceptions.feedback: A chain runs each call once, in order. This loop goes round again until the critic accepts.
Voting runs the same task several times side by side. Here one call judges another's output.

questions.prompt: A lead agent spends 12 thousand tokens on its plan, each of its three workers spends 25 thousand, and the lead spends 8 thousand on the synthesis. A colleague says the lead is the expensive part. Where do most of the 95 thousand tokens go?
hints: Add the lead's two stages first.
Multiply the workers' share by the number of workers and compare.
questions.onCorrect: The workers account for 75 thousand tokens and the lead's two stages for 20 thousand, so adding workers is what drives the cost.

acceptedIdeas: To the three workers, 75 thousand of the 95 thousand
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: To the three workers, 75 thousand of the 95 thousand

choices.label: To the lead, which runs in two stages and sets the whole plan
To the three workers, 75 thousand of the 95 thousand
Evenly across the four agents, about 24 thousand tokens each

misconceptions.feedback: The lead's two stages come to 20 thousand tokens, about a fifth of the run.
The workers use 25 thousand each and the lead 20 thousand in all, so the split is not even.

questions.prompt: A multi-agent run used 100 thousand tokens, and a single agent working serially would have needed about 35 thousand. How many times as many tokens does the multi-agent run use as the single agent? Give it to one decimal place.
hints: Divide the multi-agent total by the single agent's total.
Both are in thousands of tokens, so the units cancel.
Divide 100 by 35 on a calculator and round to one decimal place.
questions.onCorrect: The comparison is a ratio of totals, and it should be set against what the extra tokens buy in time and quality.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 100 ÷ 35 is about 2.857, which is 2.9 to one decimal place.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how many thousand tokens more the multi-agent run uses. The question asks for a ratio.
That divides the single agent's total by the multi-agent total. Put the multi-agent total on top.

questions.prompt: A worker reads 18,000 tokens of web pages and returns a summary of 600 tokens to its lead. What can the lead know about those pages?
hints: Ask what actually arrives in the lead's context.
questions.onCorrect: The small summary is what keeps the lead's context small, and it is also why the lead cannot answer a question about a detail that the summary dropped.

acceptedIdeas: Only what the summary kept, a small part of what the worker read
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only what the summary kept, a small part of what the worker read

Everything in them, since the summary was written from the pages
Only what the summary kept, a small part of what the worker read

questions.prompt: A lead briefs four workers. It could give each the whole research question and everything gathered so far, 30,000 tokens, or a narrow brief of 500 tokens for that worker's search. What is the main cost of the first choice?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each worker reads 30,000 tokens it mostly does not need, 120,000 in all

choices.label: The agent contract rejects any brief that long
Nothing, since the workers run in parallel and parallel work costs nothing
Each worker reads 30,000 tokens it mostly does not need, 120,000 in all

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing in a contract forbids a long brief. It is allowed and wasteful.
Parallel work finishes sooner, but every worker's tokens are still billed.

questions.prompt: A team builds a lead and three workers to answer questions about one 20-page policy document. The whole document fits easily in one context, and each question needs one or two sections. What should the team do?
hints: Ask whether the work can be split into parts that run side by side, and whether the material is larger than one context.

questions.onCorrect: Several agents pay off for broad searches that run in parallel or material that exceeds one context. A short document that one agent can read is not that case.

acceptedIdeas: Use one agent, since there is nothing to split and extra agents add cost
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Use one agent, since there is nothing to split and extra agents add cost

choices.label: Keep the workers but remove the lead so they work without one
Keep the lead and workers, since more agents give better answers
Use one agent, since there is nothing to split and extra agents add cost
Give each worker a full copy of the document so none is short of context

misconceptions.feedback: Without a lead nothing divides the work or combines the answers, and the document still gives nothing to split.
Anthropic's account of its research system ties the benefit to heavy parallel work and to material larger than one context window. Neither is true here.
Three copies cost three times the tokens to answer a question that one agent can read once.

questions.prompt: What is the likely outcome, and what is the remedy?
hints: Think about what happens when two writers each start from the same version of a file.
The contract should say who may write.
questions.onCorrect: Shared mutable state needs an owner, because two writers that start from the same version can overwrite each other's work.

acceptedIdeas: One save may overwrite another, so give the list a single owner
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: One save may overwrite another, so give the list a single owner

choices.label: All the sources are kept, because each worker only adds to the list
The list grows without limit, so give each worker a smaller budget
One save may overwrite another, so give the list a single owner
Nothing goes wrong, because the workers use different tools

misconceptions.feedback: Each worker saves the whole list as it read it plus its own sources, so a save can erase what another worker added in the meantime.
A smaller budget does not change what happens when two saves collide.
The tools make no difference. The fault lies in several saves of the same list.

questions.prompt: A lead tells each of three workers "research the semiconductor shortage" and nothing more. The workers come back with overlapping findings and none of them covers the 2021 factory fires. What is the likeliest cause?
hints: A worker holds only its brief and its own searches. What did these briefs say?

questions.onCorrect: Anthropic reports that without detailed task descriptions agents duplicate work, leave gaps or fail to find what is needed. A good brief gives each worker a goal, a return format, the tools and sources to use, and a clear scope.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The briefs gave no goal, scope or sources, so workers duplicated work and left a gap

choices.label: The workers ran at the same time, and workers that run in parallel always overlap
The briefs gave no goal, scope or sources, so workers duplicated work and left a gap
The lead's model was too small to plan the task, so a larger one is needed
The workers share one context, so each repeated what the others had found

misconceptions.feedback: Running at the same time does not cause overlap. Workers given distinct, bounded tasks can search in parallel without repeating each other.
Planning is not the fault here. The workers' tasks were never written down, and a larger model would still pass on the same one-line brief.
A worker does not share the lead's context or the other workers'. That isolation is why the brief has to carry everything.

questions.prompt: A lead's contract says every worker must return a JSON object with a `claim` field and a `url` field, and the lead rejects anything else. Which part of the contract is this?

misconceptions.feedback: The input is what the lead sends the worker. This rule is about what comes back.

questions.prompt: A lead writes the contract for a research worker. Which part of the contract holds each of these rules?

items.label: The question about last year's churn and the two source addresses to start from

items.label: A list of claims, each with a source address and a rating of high, medium or low
items.explanation: It fixes the shape of the reply so that the lead can check it.

items.label: Search and read web pages, but send no email and write no files
items.explanation: It names what the worker may call.

items.explanation: It is part of the task that the worker is given.
